  X.X.X.X:5000 → Invalid syntax for traceroute — it takes host, not host:port

examTip: nc -v host port is the general-purpose way to test whether a specific TCP port is reachable and accepting connections — works for arbitrary application ports, not just well-known services.

q: Users are unable to ping hosts on the same network segment using their hostname: # ping host1 ping: host1: Temporary failure in name resolution Users are only able to reach the hosts when using their FQDN, such as host1.comptia.local. A Linux administrator connects to the system and obtains the following output: Which of the following actions should the administrator take to resolve the issue?

options.B: Add the search domain to the network configuration
options.C: Add another DNS server entry to /etc/resolv.conf
options.D: Add a DNS A record for the specific hosts

explanation: Short hostnames fail but FQDNs work because the system is missing a configured search domain that would auto-append the domain suffix. Adding the search domain to network config fixes this exactly.

optExpl.A: /etc/hosts.allow is for TCP wrappers access control — it doesn't add domain search suffixes that fix short-name resolution.
optExpl.B: Adding the search domain (e.g., 'search comptia.local') to the network configuration means short names like 'host1' automatically get the suffix appended, enabling resolution without the full FQDN.
optExpl.C: Adding another DNS server doesn't fix the search domain issue — the problem is the suffix isn't being appended, not that the resolver is unreachable.
optExpl.D: Adding a specific A record for each host is impractical and doesn't fix the underlying missing search domain for all hosts.

examTip: Resolving short hostnames (not FQDNs) on the same network relies on a configured DNS search domain being appended automatically — add the search domain rather than more nameservers or per-host DNS records.

q: Which of the following commands is used to verify whether a port is open on a remote host?
explanation: nc attempts a connection to a specific port on a remote host and reports whether it's open. ip and ping operate at lower layers without per-port detail, and netstat only shows local socket information.

optExpl.A: ip manages network interfaces, routing, and addresses — not direct port-open tests on remote hosts.
optExpl.B: ping tests ICMP reachability to a host — it has no concept of TCP/UDP ports.
optExpl.C: nc (netcat) can attempt a TCP or UDP connection to a specific port on a remote host and report whether it's open or refused.
optExpl.D: netstat shows local socket state on the current machine — it can't check whether a remote port is open.

examTip: nc (netcat) is the general tool for testing whether a specific port is open on a remote host — ping only checks basic reachability (ICMP), not any particular port or service.

q: Which of the following describes what Ansible is used for in the context of IT Infrastructure?
explanation: Ansible is used for configuration management — ensuring systems are configured to a defined, consistent desired state. Not database, process, or asset management.

optExpl.A: Database management (CRUD operations, schema design) is not Ansible's function — Ansible doesn't manage database content.
optExpl.B: Configuration management — ensuring systems are configured to a desired, consistent state — is Ansible's primary use case.
optExpl.C: Process management (starting/stopping processes) can be done by Ansible tasks but is not its defining purpose.
optExpl.D: Asset management tracks hardware/software inventory — Ansible gathers facts but isn't primarily an asset management tool.

examTip: Ansible's core job is configuration management — keeping systems in a defined, consistent state — not database, process, or asset management.

q: A Linux user needs to authenticate to a Windows Active Directory domain. Which of the following configuration files contains the domain configuration details?
explanation: sssd.conf holds the domain join and authentication configuration for integrating Linux with Active Directory/LDAP. auditd.conf governs audit logging, pam.conf relates to PAM stacks, smb.conf configures Samba file-sharing.

optExpl.A: sssd.conf (System Security Services Daemon) holds the domain name, AD/LDAP server addresses, and authentication settings for integrating a Linux system with Active Directory.
optExpl.B: auditd.conf configures the Linux audit daemon for security event logging — not domain authentication.
optExpl.C: pam.conf (or /etc/pam.d/) configures pluggable authentication modules — not the AD domain connection settings.
optExpl.D: smb.conf configures Samba's file and print sharing — while Samba can join AD, sssd.conf is the specific file for AD authentication integration.

examTip: sssd.conf configures the System Security Services Daemon, which is what actually joins/authenticates a Linux host against Active Directory — smb.conf is for file/print sharing (Samba), not domain auth.

q: Which of the following protocols is used to monitor network devices?
explanation: SNMP is specifically designed for monitoring and managing network devices by polling their status and metrics. DNS, DHCP, and SMTP serve name resolution, address assignment, and email.

optExpl.A: DNS resolves hostnames to IP addresses — it's not designed for ongoing device monitoring or polling metrics.
optExpl.B: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is specifically designed to poll and monitor the status, configuration, and metrics of network devices like switches and routers.
optExpl.C: DHCP assigns IP addresses to clients — it doesn't monitor device health or collect metrics.
optExpl.D: SMTP is the email transfer protocol — not a device monitoring protocol.

examTip: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is the standard protocol for polling and monitoring network device status/metrics — DNS/DHCP/SMTP each serve a completely different purpose.

q: Which of the following is the first step when starting a new Python project on a Linux system?
chapter: Module 13: Scripting with Bash and Python
explanation: python -m venv /path/to/project creates the virtual environment — the recommended first step for any new Python project before anything is installed.

optExpl.A: python -m venv /path/to/project creates an isolated virtual environment directory — this is the recommended first step before installing any project-specific packages.
optExpl.B: pip install -r requires.txt installs packages — this should happen after the virtual environment exists and is activated.
optExpl.C: 'export PYTHON_PATH:' is not valid shell syntax, and PYTHON_PATH is not a standard Python environment variable.
optExpl.D: 'python -m source' is not a valid Python module command.

examTip: python -m venv creates an isolated virtual environment — the conventional first step of any new Python project, done before installing any dependencies into it.

q: Which of the following Linux directories contains documentation for installed software packages and shareable system files?
explanation: /usr holds shareable read-only data including documentation for installed packages under /usr/share/doc. /lib has shared libraries, /var has variable runtime data, /dev has device files.

optExpl.A: /lib holds essential shared libraries needed for boot and basic system operation — not documentation.
optExpl.B: /var holds variable data like logs, mail spools, and databases — not static package documentation.
optExpl.C: /usr holds shareable, read-only user data including installed programs and their documentation (typically under /usr/share/doc).
optExpl.D: /dev holds device files (block and character devices) — not documentation.

examTip: /usr holds shareable, read-only program data including installed packages' documentation (/usr/share/doc) — distinct from /var (variable/log data) and /lib (shared libraries).

q: A systems administrator wants to update and apply changes in an existing file in a remote Git repository. Which of the following is the last Git command the administrator should execute to complete this process?
chapter: Module 13: Scripting with Bash and Python
explanation: git push origin update-feature uploads local commits to the remote repository — the final step that makes the change visible. commit/checkout/pull happen earlier to prepare the change locally.

optExpl.A: git commit records changes to the local repository — it doesn't push them to the remote for others to see.
optExpl.B: git checkout -b creates a new local branch — it doesn't publish changes to the remote repository.
optExpl.C: git pull downloads remote changes to update the local branch — the opposite direction of publishing a change.
optExpl.D: git push origin update-feature uploads the local commits on 'update-feature' to the remote repository, completing the update workflow and making changes visible to others.

examTip: A typical feature-branch Git workflow ends with pushing your committed, tested changes to the remote (git push origin <branch>) — commit/pull/checkout are all steps that happen before that final push.

q: A systems administrator wants to terminate all the processes owned by testuser on a Linux VM. Which of the following should the administrator use for this task?

options.A:
for proc in $(ps | grep testuser)
do
  kill $proc
done
options.C:
for i in $(ps -ef | grep testuser | awk '{print $2}')
do
  kill -9 $i
done

explanation: killall -u testuser sends SIGTERM to all processes owned by testuser, terminating them. pkill -U terminates by UID, and the other options either check status or perform unrelated operations.

optExpl.A:
ps | grep testuser shows lines containing 'testuser' — but these include the username in the USER column AND the grep process itself. $proc would contain entire lines of text, not PIDs (Process IDs) — kill would fail.

Code shown:
  for proc in $(ps | grep testuser) → Captures entire ps output lines, not PIDs
  do kill $proc → kill expects a PID number, not a text string
  done
optExpl.B:
$user is compared with -eq (numeric equality) against the string 'testuser' — strings require = not -eq. Also, this never actually finds processes or their PIDs.

Code shown:
  while [ $user -eq 'testuser' ] → -eq is for numbers; use = for strings
  do kill $user → $user is a username string, not a PID
  done → This loop has no exit condition and would run indefinitely
optExpl.C:
Correctly extracts PIDs (Process IDs) belonging to testuser and forcibly terminates them.

Code shown:
  for i in $(ps -ef | grep testuser | awk '{print $2}') → Extracts column 2 = PID numbers
  do kill -9 $i → Sends SIGKILL (signal 9) to each PID
  done

Flag breakdown:
  ps -ef     → Process Status: -e=all processes, -f=full format (PID is column 2)
  grep testuser → Filter lines belonging to testuser
  awk '{print $2}' → Print field 2 = PID column
  kill -9    → Send signal 9 (SIGKILL — cannot be caught or ignored, forces immediate termination)
optExpl.D:
'while true; do killall; done' creates an infinite loop — killall without arguments also fails. This would spin forever consuming CPU.

Flag breakdown:
  while true → Infinite loop (no exit condition)
  killall    → Kill all processes by name — requires a process name argument
  done       → End of loop (never reached due to infinite condition)

examTip: Killing processes for a specific user by name reliably means finding their PIDs first (ps -ef | grep <user> | awk '{print $2}') and killing each one — killall/loops on non-existent conditions in the distractors don't actually target the right processes.

q: A Linux administrator attempts to unmount the local filesystem /data in order to mount a new volume. However, the administrator receives the following error message: umount: /data: target is busy Which of the following commands should the administrator run to resolve the issue?
explanation: fuser -mk identifies and kills processes holding the mount point open, directly resolving 'target is busy.' tree/ls/stat just inspect metadata without revealing or fixing which process is keeping it busy.

optExpl.A:
tree -g displays directory structure with group ownership — it shows what's there, not which processes have files open.

Flag breakdown:
  tree       → Display directory tree
  -g         → Show group ownership
optExpl.B:
ls -ld shows the directory's permissions and ownership — not which processes are holding it busy.

Flag breakdown:
  ls -l      → Long listing format
  -d         → List the directory itself (not its contents)
optExpl.C:
stat -f reports filesystem statistics (type, block size, free space) — not open file handles.

Flag breakdown:
  stat -f    → Filesystem statistics for the path
optExpl.D:
Identifies processes with open files on the mount point and optionally kills them to allow unmounting.

Flag breakdown:
  fuser      → Show which processes are USing a File/mount point
  -m         → Mount point — interpret path as a mount point and find all users
  -k         → Kill — send SIGKILL to all processes using the mount point
  /data      → The mount point that's reported as busy
  (Use fuser /data first to see what's using it, then -k to kill those processes)

examTip: fuser -mk <mountpoint> both identifies and kills whatever process(es) are holding a filesystem open — the direct fix for "target is busy" on umount, faster than manually cross-referencing lsof.

q: While reviewing local accounts on a server, a Linux administrator discovers that multiple users have not changed their passwords in more than a year. Which of the following commands should the administrator execute to bring the users' accounts into compliance with the 90-day guideline?
explanation: chage -M 90 sets the maximum password age, bringing accounts into compliance with a 90-day policy. usermod -aG adds group membership, passwd -d removes the password entirely, and loginctl manages sessions.

optExpl.A:
Sets the maximum password age to 90 days, forcing password change within that window.

Flag breakdown:
  chage      → CHange AGE — modify password expiry information
  -M 90      → Maximum days: password expires after 90 days
  (Other useful chage flags:
   -m N  → Minimum days between changes
   -W N  → Warning days before expiry
   -I N  → Inactive days after expiry before account locks
   -l user → List current aging info for a user)
optExpl.B:
usermod -aG tries to add the user to a supplementary group — '90' would be interpreted as a group name, not a number of days.

Flag breakdown:
  usermod    → Modify user account properties
  -aG 90     → Append to Group named '90' (not related to password aging)
optExpl.C:
passwd -d deletes a user's password (makes account passwordless) — completely different from setting an expiry.

Flag breakdown:
  passwd -d  → Delete/remove the password hash (leaves account with no password)
optExpl.D:
loginctl manages login sessions via systemd-logind — not password aging policies.

Flag breakdown:
  loginctl   → Control the systemd login manager
  -H         → Host to connect to (remote operation flag)

examTip: chage -M <days> sets the maximum password age (forced expiry interval) for an account — the tool for enforcing a "password must be changed every N days" policy.

q: A systems administrator is restoring data from a backup. While analyzing the file format, the administrator sees the following output: data: 7-zip archive data, version 0.4 Which of the following commands should the administrator use to help extract the data?
explanation: 7za e extracts 7-zip archives using the p7zip tool that natively handles the 7z format. tar/unzip/zcat are built for different formats.

optExpl.A: 7za e (from the p7zip package) extracts a 7-zip archive — identified by the file command as '7-zip archive data'.
optExpl.B: tar with --lzip handles lzip-compressed tarballs — not 7-zip format files.
optExpl.C: unzip handles ZIP format files — not 7-zip archives.
optExpl.D: zcat decompresses gzip-format files — not 7-zip archives.

examTip: Identify a file by its actual content (`file` reporting "7-zip archive data"), not its filename — the matching extraction tool (7za e/x) is the one built for that specific archive format, regardless of what extension the file was given.

q: A Linux administrator is configuring a CUPS print service on a Linux machine and needs to allow only connections from a local network. Which of the following commands should the administrator use?
explanation: iptables -A INPUT -s 192.168.100.0/24 --dport 631 -p tcp -j ACCEPT puts the rule in the INPUT chain (incoming connections) and scopes it to the source subnet. OUTPUT governs traffic leaving the host, and -D deletes rules.

optExpl.A:
OUTPUT chain governs packets LEAVING this host — wrong direction for accepting incoming print requests from remote clients.

Flag breakdown:
  iptables   → IP packet filtering and NAT tool
  -A OUTPUT  → Append to OUTPUT chain (for traffic LEAVING this machine — wrong!)
  -d 192.168.100.0/24 → Destination network (where traffic is GOING TO)
  --sport 631 → Source port 631 (where traffic COMES FROM)
  -p tcp     → TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) protocol
  -j ACCEPT  → Jump to ACCEPT action
optExpl.B:
Also uses the OUTPUT chain — still wrong direction. Source/destination flags are correct but chain is wrong.

Flag breakdown:
  -A OUTPUT  → OUTPUT chain = outgoing traffic FROM this host (not incoming print jobs)
  -s 192.168.100.0/24 → Source network (where traffic comes FROM — correct)
  --dport 631 → Destination port 631 (CUPS port — correct)
  (Chain should be INPUT to accept incoming connections to this host)
optExpl.C:
Correct chain (INPUT) and correct source scoping — allows only that subnet's print requests through.

Flag breakdown:
  iptables   → Netfilter packet filtering tool
  -A INPUT   → Append to INPUT chain (traffic arriving AT this machine — correct!)
  -s 192.168.100.0/24 → Source: only from this network (192.168.100.x addresses)
  --dport 631 → Destination Port 631 = CUPS (Common Unix Printing System)
  -p tcp     → Protocol: TCP
  -j ACCEPT  → Jump: ACCEPT this traffic
  (/24 = 256 addresses, subnet mask 255.255.255.0)
optExpl.D:
-D INPUT deletes a matching rule — not adds one.

Flag breakdown:
  -D         → Delete a matching rule from the chain
  -d 192.168.100.0/24 → Destination network (should be -s for source)
  (You want -A to Append, not -D to Delete)

examTip: iptables direction matters: -A INPUT with -s <source network> --dport <service port> is how you restrict who's allowed to *connect in*; OUTPUT rules and --sport target the wrong direction/field entirely.

q: A systems administrator is investigating bandwidth issues on a Linux file server that should be able to easily exceed 12.5MBps. The administrator inspects the following information: Which of the following is causing the bandwidth issue?

options.A: The network interface enp1s0f0 is not using FEC mode
options.B: The network interface enp1s0f0 has the incorrect queue length configured
options.C: The network interface negotiated speed for enp1s0f0 is set too low
options.D: The network interface enp1s0f0 has misconfigured the MTU value

explanation: If the NIC negotiated a lower link speed (e.g., 100Mbps instead of 1Gbps), that directly caps achievable throughput below 12.5MBps. FEC mode, queue length, and MTU affect performance differently.

optExpl.A: FEC (Forward Error Correction) mode affects signal reliability at very high speeds — its absence doesn't directly cap throughput at 12.5MBps.
optExpl.B: Queue length affects burst buffering but doesn't create a hard speed ceiling like a link speed negotiation does.
optExpl.C: If the NIC negotiated a lower link speed (e.g., 100Mbps = 12.5MBps max) instead of 1Gbps, that directly caps achievable throughput — matching the symptom exactly.
optExpl.D: MTU misconfiguration causes fragmentation overhead, reducing effective throughput somewhat — but doesn't usually create a hard ceiling matching exactly 12.5MBps.

examTip: A negotiated link speed lower than the interface's rated capability (visible in ethtool output) caps real-world throughput well below what the hardware should support — check negotiated Speed before suspecting MTU, duplex, or FEC.

q: Users are unable to access a server after it is restarted. However, an administrator is able to connect directly to the server through a console in the server room and sees the following: Which of the following is the most likely reason for this connectivity issue?

options.A: The server has no issue with the network and should be restarted to restore functionality
options.B: The server networking cable is plugged into the wrong interface and needs to be moved
options.C: The server is not able to obtain an IP address from the DHCP server
options.D: The server's network card has failed and will need to be replaced with a new networking card

explanation: If the server can't get an IP from DHCP after restart, it has no network address and becomes unreachable — while still accessible directly at the console. A bad cable, failed NIC, or 'just restart' show different symptoms.

optExpl.A: If the server had no network issue, remote users would be able to connect — they can't, so there is a network issue.
optExpl.B: A cable in the wrong interface would prevent any network communication — but the admin can access the server at the console and the interface shows UP.
optExpl.C: If the server can't reach a DHCP server after restart, it doesn't obtain an IP address and becomes unreachable remotely — while still functioning locally at the console.
optExpl.D: A failed NIC would show the interface as DOWN or missing — and would likely produce hardware errors in dmesg.

examTip: A server with an active link but no IP address, that only responds on the local console, is almost always failing to get a lease from DHCP — not a cabling or NIC hardware failure.

q: A Linux administrator is concerned about corruption of the partition table and wants to make a backup. Which of the following should the administrator use?
explanation: dd copies raw partition table data (which lives outside any filesystem) block by block. cpio, gzip, and tar operate at the file level and don't capture the partition table.

optExpl.A:
cpio archives files at the filesystem level — it cannot capture the raw partition table stored in the disk's MBR or GPT header area.

Flag breakdown:
  cpio       → Copy In/Out — file-level archiving (misses raw disk structures)
optExpl.B:
gzip compresses a single file or stream — it's not a block-level disk imaging tool.

Flag breakdown:
  gzip       → GNU zip compression — works on files, not raw block devices for imaging
optExpl.C:
tar archives files and directories at the filesystem level — the partition table exists outside any filesystem and won't be captured.

Flag breakdown:
  tar        → Tape Archive — file-level tool (misses GPT/MBR partition table data)
optExpl.D:
Performs a raw, block-level copy of the entire disk including the partition table (MBR or GPT), boot sectors, and all data exactly as stored on disk.

Flag breakdown:
  dd         → Disk Dump — block-level copy tool (copies bytes, not files)
  if=/dev/sda → Input File: source disk device (entire physical disk)
  of=/tmp/sda_backup → Output File: destination image file
  (MBR = Master Boot Record, GPT = GUID Partition Table — stored in first 512B–1MB of disk)
  (dd captures EVERYTHING on the disk byte-for-byte — partition table, boot code, all data)

examTip: dd captures a raw, byte-for-byte image of a whole disk including the partition table itself — exactly what you need to back up or restore partition table structure, unlike file-oriented tools (tar/cpio/gzip).

q: Which of the following is the best way to create a non-interactive account in a Linux system?

options.B: By using adduser with no password

explanation: Setting the shell to /sbin/nologin prevents interactive sessions while still allowing the account to exist for service purposes. No privileges, no password, or no home directory alone don't stop interactive login.

optExpl.A: Having no elevated privileges is a good security practice but doesn't prevent interactive login — the account can still start a shell.
optExpl.B: No password (adduser with no password) might allow empty-password login depending on PAM config, but doesn't reliably prevent all interactive login methods.
optExpl.C: No home directory means no persistent user files, but the account can still log in and use /tmp or other directories.
optExpl.D: Setting the shell to /sbin/nologin makes the shell produce a 'this account is not available' message and exit immediately — preventing any interactive shell session regardless of authentication method.

examTip: A non-interactive/service account should have its shell set to /sbin/nologin so no one can get an interactive session from it, even with valid credentials.

q: An administrator receives a report that a user is unable to execute the run report Ñ utility that is used to generate weekly reports. The administrator logs in as the user to verify the issue, runs the following commands, and receives the following output: Which of the following best describes the issue and how to resolve it?

options.A: The runreports utility is not in the user's PATH. The administrator should modify the .bash_profile file.
options.B: The runreports utility is a shell script, but not owned by the user, and is therefore unable to be run. The administrator should use the chown command.
options.C: The user does not have the correct SELinux context to use the runreports utility. The administrator should modify the SELinux template.
options.D: The runreports utility does not have execute permissions for the user. The administrator should add execute permissions for the user.

explanation: If the script's directory isn't in $PATH the shell can't find it by name — adding it via .bash_profile fixes that persistently. Ownership issues, SELinux context, and missing execute bits produce different specific errors.

optExpl.A: If runreports isn't in a directory listed in the user's $PATH, the shell can't find it by name — modifying .bash_profile to add its directory to PATH fixes that.
optExpl.B: chown changes ownership — but if it's a PATH issue, the user might be running the wrong binary or none at all; ownership isn't the described cause.
optExpl.C: An SELinux context problem would produce a specific denial message in audit logs — not the symptom of 'unable to execute' due to PATH.
optExpl.D: Missing execute permissions would produce 'Permission denied' — but the question says the admin logged in as the user and ran commands, suggesting a PATH issue from the output.

examTip: "Command not found" for a script that clearly exists and is executable usually means its directory isn't in $PATH — fix that in a shell startup file like .bash_profile rather than chasing ownership or permissions.

q: An administrator wants to see all logs for the app.service systemd process. Which of the following commands should the administrator use to complete this task?
explanation: journalctl -u app.service filters the journal to only that unit's entries. cat /var/log/messages is generic/unfiltered, and the other commands report status/analysis, not log history.

optExpl.A:
cat /var/log/messages shows unfiltered system log output — on systemd-only systems this file may not exist at all.

Flag breakdown:
  cat        → Display file contents
  /var/log/messages → Traditional syslog file (not present on all systemd systems)
optExpl.B:
systemctl status shows current state and only the last ~10 log lines — not the complete log history.

Flag breakdown:
  systemctl status → Shows: Active/inactive, last few log lines, process info
  (Use journalctl for complete log history)
optExpl.C:
systemd-analyze unit-files checks unit file configuration health — it's not a log viewer.

Flag breakdown:
  systemd-analyze unit-files → Lists unit files with their state (enabled/disabled/static)
optExpl.D:
Filters the systemd journal to show only log entries generated by app.service.

Flag breakdown:
  journalctl → Journal Control — query the systemd journal (centralized log store)
  -u app.service → Unit filter: show only entries from this specific service unit
  (Other useful journalctl flags:
   -f        → Follow (like tail -f — real-time stream)
   -n 50     → Last 50 lines
   --since 'today' → Filter by time
   -p err    → Only errors and above)

examTip: journalctl -u <unit> filters the systemd journal down to just that one service's log entries — the direct way to see "all logs" for a specific unit, unlike grepping a shared log file.

q: Which of the following is an example of an AI best practice?

options.C: Sampling a group of similar users when creating the model

chapter: Module 13: Scripting with Bash and Python
explanation: Sanitizing sensitive data before sending it to a public AI tool is a core responsible-use practice. Pasting directly into a terminal, sampling similar users, and blanket-linting proprietary code are risky or careless practices.

optExpl.A: Copy-pasting AI output directly into a terminal without review is dangerous — it can execute unreviewed commands with immediate consequences.
optExpl.B: Sanitizing sensitive data before sending it to an AI tool (especially a public one) prevents confidential information from being exposed to third-party systems.
optExpl.C: Sampling similar users when building AI models can introduce bias — it's the opposite of a best practice for representative model training.
optExpl.D: Always linting proprietary source code in a public AI tool exposes intellectual property — the 'always' makes it a bad practice even if occasional linting might be acceptable with proper controls.

examTip: Responsible AI use means scrubbing sensitive/identifying data before it ever reaches the model — sanitizing input, not blind copy-paste or lint-everything-automatically habits.

q: System users are being randomly disconnected from a server. The systems administrator inspects the following output: Which of the following should the administrator do to fix the issue?
explanation: A failing NIC causes intermittent random disconnects — replacing the hardware resolves a physical failure. A missing gateway, low TTL, or wrong MTU cause complete failure or specific performance problems, not random drops.

optExpl.A: A missing gateway would cause complete failures to reach outside subnets — not random disconnections while other traffic works.
optExpl.B: A failing NIC (hardware failure) causes intermittent, unpredictable connection drops — random disconnections that can't be explained by configuration issues point to hardware.
optExpl.C: Increasing ping's TTL affects how far ICMP packets travel — it doesn't fix physical NIC failures causing random disconnects.
optExpl.D: MTU size affects packet fragmentation — MTU issues cause specific performance or connectivity problems, not random disconnections.

examTip: Random disconnects with otherwise-normal configuration (routing/MTU/TTL fine) point at a flaky physical NIC — hardware replacement, not a settings tweak.

q: A user reports recurrent issues with an application, which is currently operational. The systems administrator gathers the following outputs to diagnose the issue: Which of the following is a possible cause of this issue?

options.A: A backup is consuming all the system memory.
options.B: The system is using all the swap
options.C: The cached memory is approaching the system's limits.
options.D: The process is showing signs of a memory leak.

chapter: Module 8: Managing the Linux Kernel and Devices
explanation: Memory usage growing over time in an otherwise operational application is a classic early-stage memory leak — the process slowly consuming more than it releases. A backup, swap exhaustion, or high cache wouldn't tie to one app's growing footprint.

optExpl.A: Backup processes consume resources temporarily and at scheduled times — not a continuous growing memory pattern.
optExpl.B: Swap usage being high means physical RAM is exhausted and paging is occurring — but this is a consequence of high memory use, not the root cause.
optExpl.C: Cache memory approaching limits is normal kernel behavior — the kernel evicts cache freely to give memory to processes; high cache isn't itself a problem.
optExpl.D: A process whose memory usage grows continuously over time despite being otherwise operational is the classic definition of a memory leak — it allocates memory it never frees.

examTip: Watch for the specific phrase "memory usage climbing over time" in a still-running process — that's a memory leak, distinct from swap exhaustion or cache growth (which self-manages and isn't a leak).

q: Application owners are reporting that their application stops responding after several days of running, and they need to restart it. A Linux administrator obtains the following details from the dmesg command: The application owners mentioned that resources to the system have boon increased, and the error takes longer to appear. Which of the following best describes the reason the process is being terminated by OOM?

options.A: The CPU type is incompatible with the application.
options.C: The application might have a memory leak.
options.D: The swap configuration is not correctly sized.

chapter: Module 8: Managing the Linux Kernel and Devices
explanation: Being OOM-killed after a longer delay even after resources were increased strongly suggests a memory leak — more memory just takes longer to exhaust. CPU incompatibility, a kernel panic, or wrong swap sizing wouldn't be 'delayed' by simply adding more memory.

optExpl.A: CPU incompatibility would cause crashes or failures immediately or on specific operations — not a gradual days-long memory exhaustion pattern.
optExpl.B: A kernel panic halts the entire system — the question describes a specific application becoming unresponsive, not a system-wide failure.
optExpl.C: An application that runs longer without failure after resources are increased (because it takes longer to exhaust more memory) is a strong indicator of a memory leak — more resources just delay the inevitable.
optExpl.D: Swap misconfiguration affects what happens after RAM is exhausted — it doesn't change the pattern of memory growing continuously over days.

examTip: OOM-killer terminations that take *longer* to trigger after adding more RAM (rather than never happening) confirm a genuine memory leak — more memory just buys time before the same leak eventually exhausts it again.

q: A systems administrator is creating a now shared directory. Which of the following commands ensures all users from the same group will be able to work with the newly created files?
explanation: chmod g+s (setgid bit) makes every new file in the directory inherit the directory's group, so all group members can work with new files regardless of who created them. Just adding r/w/x bits controls existing access but not future file ownership.

optExpl.A:
chmod g+r adds group read permission to existing files — it doesn't affect what group future files automatically inherit.

Flag breakdown:
  chmod g+r  → Grant Read permission to Group for existing files only
optExpl.B:
The setgid bit on a directory causes new files and subdirectories created inside to automatically inherit the directory's group ownership.

Flag breakdown:
  chmod g+s /shared → Set the SGID (Set Group ID) bit on the directory
  Effect: new files created inside inherit the DIRECTORY's group (not the creator's primary group)
  Example: if /shared has group 'project', all new files get group 'project' automatically
  (Verify with: ls -ld /shared — you'll see 's' in the group execute position: drwxrwsr-x)
optExpl.C:
chmod g+w adds group write permission to existing files — doesn't affect future file group ownership.

Flag breakdown:
  chmod g+w  → Grant Write permission to Group for existing files only
optExpl.D:
chmod g+x adds group execute permission to the directory (traversal) — doesn't affect new file group ownership.

Flag breakdown:
  chmod g+x  → Grant eXecute/traverse permission to Group for directory entry only

examTip: chmod g+s on a directory (setgid) makes every new file/subdirectory created inside automatically inherit the directory's group — the standard fix for shared-directory group-ownership headaches.

q: The development team asks a Linux administrator to help diagnose a connectivity issue that is occurring with a newly developed software. The Linux administrator reviews the following output: Which of the following actions is a best way to resolve the issue?

options.A: Verify the remote certificate is trustworthy, and add it to the local trusted certificates repository.
options.B: Replace the remote certificate with a now self-signed CA and application certificate.
options.C: Replace the expired CA certificate to permanently resolve the problem.
options.D: Add option no check certificate to wget command to permanently resolve the problem.

explanation: Verifying the remote certificate is legitimate and adding it to the local trust store is the correct fix. Replacing certificates that may be fine or adding no-check-certificate just suppresses the warning rather than actually fixing trust.

optExpl.A: The correct fix is to verify the remote certificate is legitimate, then add it to the local certificate trust store — this establishes genuine trust rather than suppressing warnings.
optExpl.B: Replacing the remote certificate with a new self-signed one doesn't fix the trust problem unless the new self-signed CA is also added to the local trust store.
optExpl.C: If the CA certificate isn't expired (the question describes a connectivity issue, not expiry), replacing it is unnecessary and disruptive.
optExpl.D: Adding --no-check-certificate to wget permanently bypasses all TLS validation — this 'fixes' the symptom by removing security entirely, not by establishing real trust.

examTip: Certificate trust errors for a server you actually intend to trust are fixed by importing that certificate into your local trusted store — not by disabling cert checking or minting a new self-signed cert.

q: A small group of remote users needs permission to run some administrative commands on a Linux server. Which of the following approaches is the best way to address this request?

options.A: Set the sticky bit in all binaries requested for use by this group of users.
options.B: Request a list of utilities they need to use with elevated privileges, and add the appropriate rules.
options.C: Set the configuration parameter PermitRootLogin on sshd_config to "yes" and share the root password with this group of users.
options.D: Create a Linux group, add the users, and configure this group on /etc/sudoers to use sudo, thus allowing them to switch to root user.

explanation: Gathering the specific privileged commands needed and granting exactly those via sudoers follows least privilege. Sharing the root password, allowing root SSH, or setting sticky bits on binaries are all far less secure.

optExpl.A: Setting the sticky bit on binaries restricts who can delete them — it doesn't grant users the ability to execute those binaries with elevated privileges.
optExpl.B: Getting a list of the specific utilities they need, then granting exactly those via sudoers entries, follows the principle of least privilege — minimum necessary access, nothing more.
optExpl.C: PermitRootLogin yes in sshd_config allows root SSH login for everyone — far too broad and a serious security risk.
optExpl.D: Simply creating a group and adding users doesn't grant elevated privileges unless the group is also configured in sudoers — this option as stated is incomplete.

examTip: Granting a few specific privileged commands to a small group means scoping sudo rules to exactly those utilities — not sharing the root password, not blanket full-root sudo access, and not sticky bits (which do something unrelated).

q: An administrator wants to start an Ubuntu terminal in a container. Which of the following will allow the administrator to complete the task?
explanation: docker run -it ubuntu starts a new container from the Ubuntu image with an interactive terminal. podman pull only downloads, containerd isn't directly invoked this way, and runc exec targets an existing container.

optExpl.A: podman pull only downloads the Ubuntu image to local storage — it doesn't start a container or provide an interactive terminal.
optExpl.B: docker run -it ubuntu creates a new container from the Ubuntu image and immediately attaches an interactive (-i) terminal (-t) — the standard way to get a shell in a fresh container.
optExpl.C: containerd is a container runtime daemon — it's not directly invoked via CLI to start interactive containers.
optExpl.D: rune exec targets an already-running container — it can't create a new one, and 'rune' is not a standard container management tool.

examTip: docker run -it <image> starts a new container and attaches an interactive terminal to it in one step — the standard way to "start a terminal in a container."

q: A Linux administrator installed a new program inside $HOME/.local/bin and is trying to execute it without using an absolute path. Which of the following should the administrator use for this task?
chapter: Module 13: Scripting with Bash and Python
explanation: export PATH=$PATH:$HOME/.local/bin appends the directory to PATH so the new program can be found by name. Omitting the leading $ before PATH would overwrite PATH with literal text 'PATH', breaking all command lookup.

optExpl.A:
PATH=PATH:... (without $ before the first PATH) sets PATH to the literal string 'PATH:/home/...', destroying all existing PATH entries and breaking all commands.

Flag breakdown:
  PATH=PATH:... → Sets PATH to literal text 'PATH:...' — the current PATH value is NOT expanded
  (Every command would fail: 'ls: command not found')
optExpl.B:
$PATH=... tries to use the current value of $PATH as a variable name — this is invalid bash syntax.

Flag breakdown:
  $PATH=     → Cannot assign to the result of a variable expansion
optExpl.C:
Correctly appends the new directory to the existing PATH value.

Flag breakdown:
  export     → Make variable available to child processes/commands
  PATH=      → Reassign the PATH variable
  $PATH      → Expand the CURRENT value of PATH (must include $ to read current contents)
  :          → PATH separator (colon-delimited list of directories)
  $HOME/.local/bin → New directory to add ($HOME expands to /home/username)
  (Full effect: PATH='/existing/dirs:/home/username/.local/bin')
optExpl.D:
Uses a hyphen (-) instead of a colon (:) as the separator — hyphens are not PATH separators.

Flag breakdown:
  $PATH-$PATH:... → Hyphen in PATH assignment = invalid, confusing, and wrong separator

examTip: export PATH=$PATH:<newdir> appends to the existing PATH by referencing the current value with $PATH — forgetting the leading $ (just "PATH:...") breaks the assignment entirely.

q: A Linux systems administrator makes updates to systemd-managed service configuration files. Which of the following commands should the administrator execute in order to implement the changes?
explanation: systemctl daemon-reload tells systemd to re-read changed unit files before the changes can take effect. enable/start/restart act on the running state but don't reload configuration definitions.

optExpl.A:
systemctl enable marks a unit to start at boot — it does not reload changed unit file definitions from disk.

Flag breakdown:
  systemctl enable → Creates symlink in target.wants/ directory for boot-time startup
optExpl.B:
systemctl start starts a stopped unit — the new configuration isn't reloaded without daemon-reload first.

Flag breakdown:
  systemctl start → Start a stopped service (uses cached unit file, not updated disk version)
optExpl.C:
systemctl restart stops and restarts the service — but uses the cached (old) unit file unless daemon-reload ran first.

Flag breakdown:
  systemctl restart → Stop + start the service
  (If you restart without daemon-reload first, the OLD configuration is still active)
optExpl.D:
Tells systemd to re-read all unit files from disk, picking up any configuration changes.

Flag breakdown:
  systemctl      → systemd (System and Service Manager) control tool
  daemon-reload  → Re-scan all unit files in /etc/systemd/system/, /lib/systemd/system/, etc.
  (Does NOT restart any services — only refreshes systemd's knowledge of unit file contents)
  (Typical workflow: edit .service file → systemctl daemon-reload → systemctl restart service)

examTip: Editing a systemd unit file only changes it on disk — systemctl daemon-reload is required before systemd notices the edit; restart/start/enable act on the old, cached unit definition until then.

q: Which of the following Ansible components is used to define groups and individual hosts and can include variables specific to each host or group?
explanation: An Ansible Inventory lists managed hosts and groups. A Playbook holds tasks, a Fact is gathered host data, and a Collection is a packaged bundle of roles/modules.

optExpl.A: Ansible Modules are the units of work (like 'apt', 'copy', 'service') that tasks call — not host and group definitions.
optExpl.B: The Ansible Inventory defines groups of hosts, individual hosts within those groups, and variables specific to each host or group.
optExpl.C: Playbooks define the tasks to run against the hosts in the inventory — they use the inventory but don't define it.
optExpl.D: Handlers are special tasks that run in response to change notifications from other tasks — not host definitions.

examTip: Ansible's Inventory defines which hosts/groups exist and can carry per-host or per-group variables — Playbooks define what to *do* to them, a different concept entirely.

q: Which of the following commands should an administrator run to check for errors during startup?
chapter: Module 8: Managing the Linux Kernel and Devices
explanation: qemu-img is the dedicated utility for converting, resizing, and inspecting virtual disk image formats. qemu-kvm runs VMs, and qemu-io/qemu-ng aren't conversion tools.

optExpl.A:
modinfo displays detailed information about a kernel module (version, description, parameters) — not startup or boot-time error logs.

Flag breakdown:
  modinfo    → Module Information — shows metadata for a kernel module file
optExpl.B:
Shows the kernel ring buffer including all messages generated during boot — hardware detection, driver loading, and any errors.

Flag breakdown:
  dmesg      → Display kernel Message buffer (ring buffer of kernel log messages)
  (Useful flags:
   dmesg -T  → Human-readable timestamps
   dmesg -l err → Only error messages
   dmesg | grep -i error → Filter for errors)
  (Startup errors appear here: disk controller issues, USB detection failures, driver errors)
optExpl.C:
dracut is a tool for building initramfs (initial RAM filesystem) images — not for reviewing startup logs.

Flag breakdown:
  dracut     → Create initramfs (initial RAM Disk) images for the boot process
optExpl.D:
lshw lists hardware in a structured format — it shows hardware info but not error messages from the boot process.

Flag breakdown:
  lshw       → List Hardware — displays hardware configuration (CPU, RAM, disks, etc.)

examTip: dmesg surfaces kernel-level messages including boot-time errors — the first place to check for hardware/driver problems that happened during startup.

q: An administrator accidentally deleted the /boot/vmlinuz file and must resolve the issue before the server is rebooted. Which of the following commands should the administrator use to identify the correct version of this file?
explanation: Listing the installed kernel package (rpm -qa | grep kernel) identifies the correct version, then grub2-mkconfig or similar tools can regenerate the vmlinuz. Rebooting immediately would fail without the kernel file restored first.

optExpl.A:
Two commands to identify the exact kernel version before attempting recovery.

Command 1 breakdown:
  rpm        → RPM (RPM Package Manager) command
  -qa        → Query All installed packages
  | grep kernel → Filter for kernel-related packages
  (Output: kernel-5.14.0-284.11.1.el9_2.x86_64 — shows installed version)

Command 2 breakdown:
  uname      → Unix NAME — show system information
  -a         → All info (kernel name, hostname, version, hardware)
  (Shows currently running kernel version — compare with rpm output to find correct vmlinuz file)
optExpl.B:
Running a full system update and rebooting without restoring /boot/vmlinuz would fail at boot — no kernel to load.

Flag breakdown:
  yum -y update → Update all packages (but doesn't fix missing /boot/vmlinuz)
  shutdown -r now → Immediate reboot (would fail — kernel file still missing)
optExpl.C:
Checking the OS release version and running rpm -Uvh --nodeps doesn't address the specific missing kernel binary file.

Flag breakdown:
  cat /etc/centos-release → Show OS release info
  rpm -Uvh   → Upgrade/install package (needs correct RPM file specified)
  --nodeps   → Skip dependency checking (risky)
optExpl.D:
telinit 1 changes runlevel to single-user mode; restorecon fixes SELinux labels — neither restores a deleted kernel binary.

Flag breakdown:
  telinit 1  → Change to runlevel 1 (single-user emergency mode)
  restorecon → Restore SELinux contexts (unrelated to missing kernel)

examTip: rpm -qa | grep kernel (or dnf list installed kernel*) shows exactly which kernel package/version is installed, and uname -a confirms what's currently running — the safe way to identify the right vmlinuz to restore before ever risking a reboot.

q: A cloud engineer needs to change the secure remote login port from 22 to 49000. Which of the following files should the engineer modify to change the port number to the desired value?
explanation: /etc/ssh/sshd_config is the SSH daemon configuration file where the Port directive controls which port sshd listens on. /etc/host.conf, /etc/hostname, and /etc/services don't control the SSH service's listening port.

optExpl.A:
/etc/host.conf configures the legacy hostname lookup order (files vs DNS) — nothing to do with SSH.

Flag breakdown:
  /etc/host.conf → Legacy NSS (Name Service Switch) configuration
optExpl.B:
/etc/hostname stores the system's hostname (a single line) — not SSH service settings.

Flag breakdown:
  /etc/hostname → Contains just the machine's hostname (e.g., 'webserver01')
optExpl.C:
/etc/services maps service names to port numbers as a reference file — but editing it doesn't make sshd actually listen on a different port.

Flag breakdown:
  /etc/services → Read-only reference mapping service names to standard port numbers
optExpl.D:
The SSH daemon configuration file — the Port directive here controls which port sshd listens on.

Flag breakdown:
  /etc/ssh/sshd_config → SSH Daemon (sshd) configuration file
  Key directive to change:
    Port 49000  → Makes sshd listen on port 49000 instead of default 22
  (After editing, restart: systemctl restart sshd)
  (Also update firewall: ufw allow 49000/tcp)
  (sshd = SSH Daemon; SSH = Secure Shell)

examTip: Port is a Port keyword inside /etc/ssh/sshd_config — the only file of these four that actually controls which port sshd listens on.

q: A new file was added to a main Git repository. An administrator wants to synchronize a local copy with the contents of the main repository. Which of the following commands should the administrator use for this task?
chapter: Module 13: Scripting with Bash and Python
explanation: git pull fetches and merges the latest commits from the remote repository in one step. git reflog/status show local history/state without pulling anything new, and git push sends changes outward.

optExpl.A: git reflog shows the local history of HEAD movements — it doesn't download or sync with a remote repository.
optExpl.B: git pull fetches from the remote repository and merges the changes into the current local branch, syncing the new file that was added remotely.
optExpl.C: git status shows the state of the working directory and staging area — it doesn't download remote changes.
optExpl.D: git push sends local changes to the remote — the opposite direction needed here.

examTip: git pull fetches new commits from the remote and merges them into your local branch in one step — exactly "synchronize local copy with the main repo's contents."

q: A Linux administrator needs to redirect all HTTP traffic temporarily to the new proxy server 192.0.2.25 on port 3128. Which of the following commands will accomplish this task?
explanation: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -p tcp --dport 80 -j DNAT --to-destination appends a PREROUTING NAT rule redirecting incoming port 80 traffic to the new proxy. The other options use wrong ports, wrong flags, or target the wrong field (sport vs dport).

optExpl.A:
-D PREROUTING deletes a matching rule — not adds one. Also uses --sport (source port) instead of --dport (destination port).

Flag breakdown:
  -t nat     → NAT (Network Address Translation) table
  -D         → Delete a matching rule (you need -A to Append)
  PREROUTING → Intercept packets BEFORE routing decisions
  --sport 80 → Source Port 80 (where traffic COMES FROM — wrong for capturing HTTP requests)
  -j DNAT    → DNAT (Destination NAT) — rewrite destination IP:port
optExpl.B:
--dport 81 redirects port 81 traffic — HTTP uses port 80. Also uses 'top' (a process viewer) instead of 'tcp' (protocol).

Flag breakdown:
  -A PREROUTING → Append rule (correct action)
  -p top     → Typo: should be 'tcp' (Transmission Control Protocol), not 'top'
  --dport 81 → Destination Port 81 — not 80 (HTTP = HyperText Transfer Protocol, port 80)
optExpl.C:
-I inserts a rule but uses --sport (source port) — HTTP traffic is identified by its DESTINATION port (--dport 80), not where it came from.

Flag breakdown:
  -I PREROUTING → Insert rule at top of chain (instead of Append)
  -p top     → Typo: 'top' instead of 'tcp'
  --sport 80 → Source Port 80 (traffic FROM port 80, not traffic TO port 80 — wrong!)
optExpl.D:
Correctly intercepts incoming HTTP traffic and redirects it to the proxy server.

Flag breakdown:
  iptables   → Netfilter packet filter/NAT tool
  -t nat     → NAT (Network Address Translation) table (for address rewriting)
  -A PREROUTING → Append to PREROUTING chain (fires BEFORE the kernel decides where to route)
  -p tcp     → Protocol: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol)
  --dport 80 → Destination Port 80 = HTTP traffic arriving at this machine
  -j DNAT    → Jump to: DNAT (Destination NAT) action
  --to-destination 192.0.2.25:3128 → Rewrite packet's destination to proxy IP:port
  (Traffic flow: client → port 80 on this host → iptables rewrites dest → proxy at 192.0.2.25:3128)

examTip: iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING ... --dport 80 -j DNAT --to-destination redirects *incoming* traffic on port 80 to a new destination — matching source port (--sport) or the wrong chain/table would target different traffic entirely.

q: Developers have requested implementation of a persistent, static route on the application server. Packets sent over the interface eth0 to 10.0.213.5/32 should be routed via 10.0.5.1. Which of the following commands should the administrator run to achieve this goal?

options.D: ip route add 10.0.213.5/32 via 10.0.5.1 dev eth0

explanation: ip route add 10.0.213.5/32 via 10.0.5.1 dev eth0 is the correct modern syntax for adding a specific static route. The legacy route syntax shown is malformed, and writing to /proc/net/route or nmcli-style modify isn't valid for this purpose.

optExpl.A:
The legacy route command syntax shown is invalid — route -i for interface specification doesn't use this format.

Flag breakdown:
  route      → Legacy routing table tool (deprecated, replaced by 'ip route')
  -i eth0    → Not valid syntax for route's add command
optExpl.B:
'route modify' with NetworkManager-style syntax is not a valid command.

Flag breakdown:
  route modify → Not a valid command (neither legacy route nor ip route)
optExpl.C:
Echoing directly into /proc/net/route writes binary kernel data format — it's not a text file and this would corrupt the routing table.

Flag breakdown:
  /proc/net/route → Kernel routing table in binary format (not human-readable text)
optExpl.D:
Correct modern iproute2 syntax for adding a specific host route.

Flag breakdown:
  ip         → iproute2 suite (modern replacement for ifconfig/route/arp)
  route      → Subcommand: manage routing table
  add        → Add a new route
  10.0.213.5/32 → Destination: /32 = single host route (exact IP match)
  via 10.0.5.1 → Gateway: next-hop IP address
  dev eth0   → Device: send through this network interface
  (To make persistent: add to /etc/network/interfaces or NetworkManager config)

examTip: ip route add <destination>/<mask> via <gateway> dev <iface> is the modern syntax for a static route — the older `route` command and made-up flags in the distractors aren't valid ways to add a persistent route.

q: A user is asking the systems administrator for assistance with writing a script to verify whether a file exists. Given the following: Which of the following commands should replace the <CONDITIONAL> string?
chapter: Module 13: Scripting with Bash and Python
explanation: for username in $USER_LIST; do useradd -m "$username"; done correctly iterates over each name. The while/until loops shown use invalid syntax for list iteration, and select is for interactive menus.

optExpl.A: if [ -f "$filename" ]; then is correct: -f tests for a regular file, the variable is quoted to handle spaces, and the semicolon before 'then' is required.
optExpl.B: -d tests for a directory — this would copy if $filename is a directory, not a regular file as the task requires.
optExpl.C: Missing the semicolon (or newline) before 'then' is a syntax error — bash requires a separator between the ] and then.
optExpl.D: Using 'while' instead of 'then' is invalid — if statements use 'then', not 'while' (which starts a loop).

examTip: Test for a file's existence with [ -f "$var" ] — quoting the variable protects against spaces/empty values, and -f specifically checks "regular file exists," not -d (directory).

q: A Linux administrator needs to create an image named sda.img from the sda disk and store it in the /tmp directory. Which of the following commands should be used to accomplish this task?
explanation: docker run -it creates a new container from the image and attaches an interactive terminal in one step. 'start' only works on an existing container, 'build' creates an image not a container, and 'exec' requires a container already running.

optExpl.A:
The if= and of= arguments are reversed — this would WRITE the image file ONTO /dev/sda, overwriting the live disk.

Flag breakdown:
  dd of=/dev/sda if=/tmp/sda.img → Reads from the image, writes to the disk
  (This would destroy the disk — data flows: image file → disk)
optExpl.B:
Reads from the source disk and writes to the image file — correct direction for backup.

Flag breakdown:
  dd         → Disk Dump — raw block-level copy
  if=/dev/sda → Input File: source disk device (read from here)
  of=/tmp/sda.img → Output File: destination image file (write to here)
  (Data flows: disk → image file)
  (To restore: dd if=/tmp/sda.img of=/dev/sda)
  (Add bs=4M for faster copying: dd if=/dev/sda of=/tmp/sda.img bs=4M)
optExpl.C:
dd doesn't support GNU-style double-dash (--) flags for if/of — these flags use = without dashes.

Flag breakdown:
  --if=      → Invalid dd syntax (should be if= without dashes)
  --of=      → Invalid dd syntax (should be of= without dashes)
optExpl.D:
Same double-dash syntax error, plus the arguments are reversed (reads from image, writes to disk — would destroy the disk).

Flag breakdown:
  --of=/dev/sda if=/tmp/sda.img → Both invalid syntax AND reversed data direction

examTip: dd if=<source> of=<destination> — if (input file) always names what you're reading FROM, of (output file) names what you're writing TO; swapping them would overwrite your source disk instead of imaging it.

q: A systems administrator is deploying three identical, cloud-based servers. The administrator is using the following code to complete the task: Which of the following technologies is the administrator using?
explanation: semanage -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 1234 adds the new port to SELinux policy for httpd — the correct, security-best-practice fix. setsebool targets a wrong boolean, setenforce 0 disables SELinux entirely, and unmask doesn't resolve a port-labeling issue.

optExpl.A: Ansible is a configuration management tool — it configures existing infrastructure but doesn't provision cloud resources from scratch.
optExpl.B: Puppet is a configuration management tool — same limitation as Ansible for cloud resource provisioning.
optExpl.C: Chef is a configuration management tool — same limitation.
optExpl.D: Terraform is the Infrastructure as Code tool designed specifically to provision and manage cloud resources (VMs, networks, load balancers) declaratively from code.

examTip: Code that declares desired end-state infrastructure (servers, networking) for cloud providers, applied declaratively rather than as an imperative script, is Terraform's signature — distinguish it from configuration-management tools (Ansible/Puppet/Chef) that manage software *on* already-provisioned machines.

q: Which of the following technologies can be used as a central repository of Linux users and groups?
explanation: Kerberos is the ticket-based authentication protocol Windows Active Directory domains use, and Linux systems join that Kerberos realm. SSH, PAM, and Samba are all involved in Linux auth/file-sharing but Kerberos is specifically the AD-domain technology.

optExpl.A: LDAP is a directory protocol that can serve as a central repository for user identities — other services authenticate against it, making it a centralized identity source.
optExpl.B: MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication) is an authentication method requiring multiple proofs — it's not a central user identity repository.
optExpl.C: SSO (Single Sign-On) allows one login to access multiple services — it typically uses LDAP as a backend but isn't itself the identity repository.
optExpl.D: PAM is a Linux authentication framework — it can connect to LDAP but is not itself a centralized user identity store.

examTip: LDAP is the standard centralized directory service for storing and querying users/groups across a network — MFA/SSO/PAM are authentication mechanisms, not user-data repositories themselves.

q: A systems administrator is troubleshooting connectivity issues and trying to find out why a Linux server is not able to reach other servers on the same subnet it is connected to. When listing link parameters, the following is presented: Based on the output above, which of following is the MOST probable cause of the issue?

options.A: The address ac:00:11:22:33:cd is not a valid Ethernet address.
options.B: The Ethernet broadcast address should be ac:00:11:22:33:ff instead.
options.C: The network interface eth0 is using an old kernel module.
options.D: The network interface cable is not connected to a switch.

explanation: Listing each node's available interfaces, IPs, and routing table (ip addr + ip route) shows whether the nodes can see each other on the network at all. ping/traceroute/curl would test connectivity but ip commands directly show the configuration causing it.

optExpl.A: ac:00:11:22:33:cd is a valid format for an Ethernet MAC address — the format is correct even if the address seems unusual.
optExpl.B: Ethernet broadcast addresses use ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff — ac:00:11:22:33:ff is not the standard broadcast address.
optExpl.C: An old kernel module would cause the interface to not appear or have errors — not a cable connectivity issue.
optExpl.D: If the network cable isn't connected to a switch (or is unplugged), the interface shows no link — causing the connectivity issues described.

examTip: A network interface that's administratively up but shows NO-CARRIER (or similar) almost always means the cable isn't actually connected to a switch/port — check physical link state before suspecting addressing or drivers.

q: A Linux administrator was asked to run a container with the httpd server inside. This container should be exposed at port 443 of a Linux host machine while it internally listens on port 8443. Which of the following commands will accomplish this task?
explanation: podman run -d -p 443:8443 maps host port 443 to the container's internal port 8443 (-p syntax is always host_port:container_port). Option B reverses the mapping, exposing 8443 instead of 443, and -e sets environment variables, not port mappings.

optExpl.A:
Runs the container in the background and maps host port 443 to the container's internal port 8443.

Flag breakdown:
  podman     → Podman (Pod Manager) — daemonless container engine
  run        → Create and start a new container
  -d         → Detached — run in background (no interactive terminal)
  -p 443:8443 → Port mapping: HOST_PORT:CONTAINER_PORT
    443      → External port (HTTPS = HyperText Transfer Protocol Secure) on host
    8443     → Internal port the httpd service listens on inside the container
  httpd      → Container image (Apache HTTP Daemon)
optExpl.B:
-p 8443:443 reverses the mapping — exposes host port 8443 to the container's port 443. Clients would need to connect to port 8443, not 443.

Flag breakdown:
  -p 8443:443 → HOST:CONTAINER — host exposes 8443, not 443
  (Clients connecting to :443 would get 'Connection refused')
optExpl.C:
-e sets environment variables — not port mappings.

Flag breakdown:
  -e NAME=VALUE → Set an Environment variable inside the container
  (For port mapping, use -p not -e)
optExpl.D:
podman exec runs a command in an already-running container — it can't create a new container or configure port mappings.

Flag breakdown:
  podman exec → Execute a command in an EXISTING running container
  -p         → Not a valid exec flag (port mapping happens at container creation with 'run')

examTip: podman/docker run -p <host-port>:<container-port> — host port always comes first, container's internal port second; getting the order backwards exposes the wrong port entirely.

q: A Linux administrator needs to analyze a failing application that is running inside a container. Which of the following commands allows the Linux administrator to enter the running container and analyze the logs that are stored inside?
explanation: dd if=/dev/sdc of=/tmp/image performs a raw block-level copy preserving deleted/slack space for forensic analysis. cp, cpio, and tar operate at the file level and miss data outside the active filesystem.

optExpl.A:
docker run would create a brand-new container from the image — not enter the existing failing 'app' container that's already running.

Flag breakdown:
  docker run -ti → Creates NEW container with interactive terminal
  app        → Treated as image name (not existing container name)
optExpl.B:
Opens an interactive shell inside the specific already-running container, enabling direct investigation.

Flag breakdown:
  podman     → Podman container engine
  exec       → Execute a command inside a RUNNING container
  -t         → TTY (TeleTYpewriter) — allocate a pseudo-terminal
  -i         → Interactive — keep STDIN open
  Combined -ti → Gives you a live interactive shell
  app        → Name/ID of the running container to enter
  /bin/sh    → Shell to start inside the container
optExpl.C:
podman run -d creates a new detached (background) container from the image — not entering the failing existing one.

Flag breakdown:
  run -d     → Run NEW container in Detached (background) mode
  /bin/bash  → Would start bash but -d means no interactive access
optExpl.D:
docker exec -d runs a command detached (background) — no interactive terminal, opposite of what's needed for investigation.

Flag breakdown:
  exec -d    → Execute command in Detached mode (background — you won't see any output)
  /bin/bash  → Starts bash but -d means you have no way to interact with it

examTip: podman/docker exec -it <container> <shell> opens an interactive shell inside an *already-running* container to inspect logs/state live — `run` would start a brand-new container instead of entering the existing one.

q: A new Linux systems administrator just generated a pair of SSH keys that should allow connection to the servers. Which of the following commands can be used to copy a key file to remote servers? (Choose two.)
explanation: scp and ssh-copy-id are the two valid ways to copy a public key to a remote server — ssh-copy-id is purpose-built for this, and scp can manually transfer the key file. wget retrieves files (wrong direction), ssh-keygen only generates keys, ssh-keyscan collects host keys, and ftpd is a server daemon.

optExpl.A:
wget retrieves files from URLs over HTTP/HTTPS — it has no capability to copy SSH keys to remote servers.

Flag breakdown:
  wget       → Web Get — download files from web URLs (HTTP/HTTPS/FTP)
optExpl.B:
ssh-keygen generates the key PAIR — it creates new keys, it doesn't copy or install them anywhere.

Flag breakdown:
  ssh-keygen → Generate a new SSH key pair (creates private + public key files)
  (After generating, you still need ssh-copy-id or scp to deploy the public key)
optExpl.C:
ssh-keyscan collects a HOST's public keys for known_hosts — not for installing YOUR public key on a remote server.

Flag breakdown:
  ssh-keyscan → Scans and prints a host's SSH public keys
  (Purpose: populate ~/.ssh/known_hosts to verify host identity)
optExpl.D:
Purpose-built command that appends your public key to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the remote server.

Flag breakdown:
  ssh-copy-id → Securely copy your PUBLIC key to remote server's authorized_keys
  (Usage: ssh-copy-id user@remote-host)
  (Appends to ~/.ssh/authorized_keys on the remote — enables passwordless login)
optExpl.E:
ftpd is the FTP (File Transfer Protocol) Daemon — a server-side daemon, not a client tool for copying SSH keys.

Flag breakdown:
  ftpd       → FTP Server Daemon (listens for incoming FTP connections)
  (FTP is also unencrypted — inappropriate for handling SSH keys)
optExpl.F:
Secure Copy Protocol can manually transfer the public key file as a generic encrypted file copy.

Flag breakdown:
  scp        → Secure Copy Protocol — encrypted file transfer using SSH
  (Usage: scp ~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub user@remote:~/.ssh/authorized_keys)
  (Less convenient than ssh-copy-id but achieves the same result)

examTip: Getting a public key onto a remote host can be done with the purpose-built ssh-copy-id, or generically with any file-copy tool like scp — ssh-keygen/ssh-keyscan only generate/collect keys, they don't transfer files.

q: A systems administrator needs to reconfigure a Linux server to allow persistent IPv4 packet forwarding. Which of the following commands is the correct way to accomplish this task?
explanation: sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 sets the kernel parameter at runtime using the correct mechanism. Manually echoing into /proc/sys works only for the current boot and isn't the standard administrative method; firewall-cmd and systemctl don't control IP forwarding at all.

optExpl.A:
Echoing to /proc/sys/ works for the current boot only, is not the administrative standard, and has a typo (ipv_forward vs ip_forward).

Flag breakdown:
  echo 1 > /proc/sys/net/ipv4/ip_forward → Sets forwarding now but lost after reboot
  ipv_forward → Typo! Should be ip_forward (ip without the 'v')
optExpl.B:
The correct administrative command to set the IP forwarding kernel parameter.

Flag breakdown:
  sysctl     → System Control — read/write kernel parameters
  -w         → Write (set) a value
  net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 → Enable IPv4 (Internet Protocol version 4) packet forwarding
    net.ipv4   → IPv4 networking subsystem
    ip_forward → Enable routing between interfaces
    =1         → Enable (0=disabled, 1=enabled)
  (For persistence: add 'net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1' to /etc/sysctl.conf or /etc/sysctl.d/99-ipforward.conf)
optExpl.C:
firewall-cmd manages firewall rules — it cannot set kernel IP forwarding parameters.

Flag breakdown:
  firewall-cmd → firewalld client (manages iptables/nftables rules only)
optExpl.D:
ip4_forwarding is not a systemd service — IP forwarding is a kernel parameter, not a service unit.

Flag breakdown:
  systemctl start → Start a systemd service
  ipv4_forwarding → Not a real service name

examTip: sysctl -w net.ipv4.ip_forward=1 sets the live kernel parameter immediately (add it to /etc/sysctl.conf separately to make it persist across reboots) — that's the standard runtime way to enable IP forwarding, not a raw /proc echo or a firewall/service command.

q: A Linux administrator would like to use systemd to schedule a job to run every two hours. The administrator creates timer and service definitions and restarts the server to load these new configurations. After the restart, the administrator checks the log file and notices that the job is only running daily. Which of the following is MOST likely causing the issue?

options.B: The checkdiskspace.service needs to be enabled.
options.C: The OnCalendar schedule is incorrect in the timer definition.
options.D: The system-daemon services need to be reloaded.

explanation: If a timer is supposed to fire every two hours but only runs daily, the OnCalendar or OnUnitActiveSec schedule in the timer unit file is incorrect — a wrong expression fires at the wrong interval. The service not running or needing enable/reload would prevent it running at all rather than run on a different (but still working) schedule.

optExpl.A: If the service weren't running, the job simply wouldn't execute — it wouldn't run on a different (daily) schedule.
optExpl.B: If the service weren't enabled, it wouldn't auto-start — but again, it wouldn't run on a different schedule.
optExpl.C: An incorrect OnCalendar schedule would cause the timer to fire at the wrong time — but the question asks about the system daemon reload, not just the schedule.
optExpl.D: After editing a timer's unit file, systemctl daemon-reload is required for systemd to pick up the changes — without it, the old schedule remains in effect.

examTip: After changing a systemd timer/service definition, systemctl daemon-reload must run before systemd picks up the new schedule — a plain reboot alone can still leave stale cached unit state in some setups, so make reloading part of the habit.

q: An administrator needs to make some changes in the IaC declaration templates. Which of the following commands would maintain version control?

options.A: git clone https://github.com/comptia/linux+-.git git push origin
options.B: git clone https://qithub.com/comptia/linux+-.git git fetch New-Branch

explanation: Cloning the repo and creating a new branch (git checkout -b) isolates IaC edits safely before merging. Pushing immediately, fetching a non-existent branch, or just checking status don't set up a safe isolated place to make and track new changes.

optExpl.A:
git push immediately uploads changes to the main repository — no isolated branch for review and testing.

Flag breakdown:
  git clone  → Copy remote repo locally
  git push origin → Push to remote (immediately — no review branch created)
optExpl.B:
git fetch New-Branch tries to fetch a branch that doesn't exist yet — no workspace is created for safe changes.

Flag breakdown:
  git fetch  → Download remote branch tracking info (doesn't create local branch)
optExpl.C:
git status shows the current state of files — it doesn't create a branch or safe workspace.

Flag breakdown:
  git status → Shows staged/unstaged/untracked files (read-only — no changes made)
optExpl.D:
Creates an isolated local branch for IaC changes — safe to test and review before merging.

Flag breakdown:
  git clone  → Clone the repository locally
  git checkout -b update-feature → Create AND switch to new branch
    -b       → Create new Branch
    update-feature → New branch name
  (Changes stay on this branch until reviewed and merged via pull request)
  (IaC = Infrastructure as Code)

examTip: A proper Git change workflow branches off before editing (git checkout -b <branch>) so changes stay isolated and reviewable — that's the version-control best practice being tested here, not just cloning and pushing straight to the main branch.

q: An administrator attempts to rename a file on a server but receives the following error. The administrator then runs a few commands and obtains the following output: Which of the following commands should the administrator run NEXT to allow the file to be renamed by any user?
explanation: The sticky bit on the directory (drwxrwxrwt) restricts renaming/deleting files to the file's owner — chmod -t removes it, allowing any group member to rename the file. chgrp/chown change ownership not the sticky bit restriction, and the chacl syntax shown isn't valid.

optExpl.A:
chgrp changes group ownership — it doesn't touch the sticky bit that's restricting rename permissions.

Flag breakdown:
  chgrp reet files → Change group of 'files' directory to 'reet' (unrelated to sticky bit)
optExpl.B:
chacl is not a standard Linux command (it exists on IRIX/AIX); setfacl is the Linux ACL tool, but neither removes the sticky bit.

Flag breakdown:
  chacl      → Not a standard Linux command
  ACL        → Access Control List (different from sticky bit restriction)
optExpl.C:
chown changes user ownership — sticky bit is a directory attribute, not an ownership setting.

Flag breakdown:
  chown users files → Change owner of 'files' directory to 'users'
optExpl.D:
Removes the sticky bit from the directory, allowing any group member to rename files inside it.

Flag breakdown:
  chmod      → CHange MODe (file permissions)
  -t         → Remove the sticky bit (t = sTicky bit)
  files      → The target directory
  (Sticky bit effect: only the file OWNER can rename/delete their own files)
  (Without sticky bit: anyone with write permission to the directory can rename/delete files)
  (Verify with ls -ld: d=directory, t in permissions = sticky bit set)

examTip: chmod -t removes the sticky bit from a directory — with it set, only a file's owner (or root) can rename/delete it even with group write access; removing it lets any user with write access rename files.

q: Which of the following commands will display the operating system?
explanation: uname -o prints the operating system name specifically (e.g., 'GNU/Linux'). uname -n shows hostname, -s shows kernel name, and -m shows machine hardware architecture.

optExpl.A: uname -n displays the network node hostname (nodename) — not the OS name.
optExpl.B: uname -s displays the kernel name (e.g., 'Linux') — not the OS name.
optExpl.C: uname -o displays the operating system name (e.g., 'GNU/Linux') — the specific field requested.
optExpl.D: uname -m displays the machine hardware name (e.g., 'x86_64') — not the OS name.

examTip: uname's flags each report something different: -s = kernel name, -n = hostname, -o = operating system, -m = machine hardware (architecture) — memorize which letter maps to which field.

q: A systems engineer is adding a new 1GB XFS filesystem that should be temporarily mounted under /ops/app. Which of the following is the correct list of commands to achieve this goal?

options.B:
parted /dev/sdb --script mkpart primary xfs 1GB
mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb
mount /dev/sdb /opt/app
