explanation: The correct sequence is creating the partition, formatting it as XFS with mkfs.xfs, then mounting it with a plain mount command (not adding an fstab entry) since the requirement is 'temporarily mounted.' A persistent fstab entry would make it permanent, not temporary.

optExpl.A: pvcreate initialises a block device as an LVM Physical Volume — it does not create a usable filesystem. You can't mkfs directly on a PV; you need vgcreate then lvcreate first. The /dev/app path is also fabricated (real PVs are disk devices like /dev/sdb).
optExpl.B:
Two problems: (1) parted mkpart creates a partition inside /dev/sdb, producing /dev/sdb1, but the next command runs mkfs.xfs /dev/sdb — formatting the entire raw disk device, not the new partition. (2) mount /dev/sdb would mount a disk with no partition table rather than the partition. Should reference /dev/sdb1 throughout.

Concept is right (partition → format → mount) but the device names are inconsistent.
optExpl.C: lvs is the 'List Logical Volumes' command — it only displays existing LVs, it has no --create flag. The correct command to create a logical volume is lvcreate. This option uses a completely non-existent syntax.
optExpl.D:
The only syntactically correct and complete sequence for creating a 1GB LVM-based XFS filesystem and mounting it temporarily.

Flag breakdown:
  lvcreate -L 1G   → Create Logical Volume, -L = size (1 GiB)
  -n app           → Name the LV 'app'
  app_vg           → Target Volume Group (must already exist)
  /dev/app_vg/app  → Device path for the new LV (VG/LV naming)

  mkfs.xfs /dev/app_vg/app → Format the LV with XFS filesystem

  mount /dev/app_vg/app /opt/app → Mount it to /opt/app
  (No /etc/fstab entry = temporary: gone after reboot)

Note: the question says /ops/app but the options all show /opt/app — this is a typo in the source material.

examTip: Building a filesystem on LVM is a multi-step chain: lvcreate (carve the logical volume from a volume group) → mkfs (format it) → mount — skipping straight to a raw partition (parted) or inventing non-existent commands ("lvs --create") breaks the LVM abstraction the question is testing.

q: A Linux administrator recently downloaded a software package that is currently in a compressed file. Which of the following commands will extract the files?
explanation: unzip -v lists/extracts standard .zip files — the most common compressed-package format. bzip2 -z compresses rather than extracts, gzip without -d also compresses by default, and funzip handles only a narrow single-file decompression case.

optExpl.A: unzip -v lists the contents of a ZIP archive (-v for verbose) or extracts files — the correct tool for a downloaded compressed .zip package.
optExpl.B: bzip2 -z compresses a file with bzip2 — it would create a .bz2 file, not extract a downloaded package.
optExpl.C: gzip without -d compresses files — not extracts. gzip -d or gunzip would decompress, but only single .gz files, not multi-file packages.
optExpl.D: funzip extracts only the first file from a ZIP archive to stdout — not suitable for extracting a complete downloaded software package.

examTip: Match the tool to the actual compression format — unzip handles .zip archives specifically; gzip/bzip2 handle single-file .gz/.bz2 streams, not zip containers.

q: A Linux administrator is troubleshooting SSH connection issues from one of the workstations. When users attempt to log in from the workstation to a server with the IP address 104.21.75.76, they receive the following message: The administrator reviews the information below: Which of the following is causing the connectivity issue?

options.A: The workstation has the wrong IP settings.
options.C: The server's firewall is preventing connections from being made.
options.D: The server has an incorrect default gateway configuration.

explanation: The error 'Connection refused' means something on the path actively rejected the connection rather than packets timing out. The workstation output shows a valid IP and default route, so the firewall on the server side is blocking port 22. A DNS issue, high load, or wrong protocol would show different symptoms.

optExpl.A: If the workstation had wrong IP settings, it wouldn't be able to reach any host, not just this specific server.
optExpl.B: If sshd were disabled on the server, the error would be 'Connection refused' or 'No route to host' — not a firewall block pattern.
optExpl.C: A 'Connection refused' message on port 22 from the server means sshd is either not running or a firewall on the server side is blocking port 22 — the latter being the most common post-restart cause.
optExpl.D: An incorrect default gateway on the server would prevent the server from reaching outside its subnet — but users connecting to it from the same network wouldn't see a firewall-style refused connection.

examTip: SSH connection failures that get no response at all (timeout, not "connection refused") from an otherwise-reachable IP usually mean a firewall is silently dropping the traffic — refused connections would point to the service itself instead.

q: Which of the following files holds the system configuration for journal when running systemd?
explanation: /etc/systemd/journald.conf is the actual configuration file for journald — note journald (the daemon) not journalctl (the viewer). The other filenames listed are not real systemd configuration file paths.

optExpl.A: /etc/systemd/journald.conf is the actual configuration file for the systemd-journald daemon, controlling log storage, size limits, and compression settings.
optExpl.B: There is no file named /etc/systemd/systemd-journalctl.conf — journalctl is the viewer, not the daemon.
optExpl.C: /usr/lib/systemd/ holds system-provided (vendor) unit files — user configuration goes in /etc/systemd/.
optExpl.D: There is no /etc/systemd/systemd-journald.conf — the correct filename is just journald.conf, not systemd-journald.conf.

examTip: /etc/systemd/journald.conf is journald's own config file — don't confuse it with the similarly-named but non-existent "systemd-journald.conf"/"systemd-journalctl.conf" distractors.

q: A Linux administrator is tasked with creating resources using containerization. When deciding how to create this type of deployment, the administrator identifies some key features, including portability, high availability, and scalability in production. Which of the following should the Linux administrator choose for the new design?
explanation: Kubernetes provides the orchestration, portability, high availability, and scalability features described for production container workloads. Plain Docker runs containers but doesn't natively provide the orchestration/HA/scaling layer. On-prem/cloud are deployment locations, not orchestration technologies.

optExpl.A: Docker runs individual containers but doesn't natively provide orchestration, high availability, or auto-scaling across multiple hosts.
optExpl.B: On-premises systems is a deployment location, not a container orchestration technology.
optExpl.C: Cloud-based systems is also a deployment location — Kubernetes can run on cloud, but Kubernetes itself is the answer, not where it runs.
optExpl.D: Kubernetes orchestrates containers at scale, providing portability across environments, high availability through replication, and horizontal scalability — the features described.

examTip: When a scenario explicitly calls out portability + high availability + scalability *in production* for containers, that's describing container orchestration — Kubernetes, not just Docker (which runs containers but doesn't orchestrate a production cluster by itself).

q: Which of the following tools is commonly used for creating CI/CD pipelines?
explanation: Jenkins is the most well-known dedicated automation server for building CI/CD pipelines. Chef, Puppet, and Ansible are configuration management tools — they can be used within a pipeline but aren't themselves CI/CD pipeline tools.

optExpl.A: Chef is a configuration management tool (infrastructure automation) — not a CI/CD pipeline platform.
optExpl.B: Puppet is a configuration management tool — not a CI/CD pipeline tool.
optExpl.C: Jenkins is the most widely used open-source automation server for building CI/CD pipelines, running builds, tests, and deployments automatically.
optExpl.D: Ansible is a configuration management and automation tool — while it can be used within a pipeline, it is not itself a CI/CD pipeline tool.

examTip: Jenkins is the classic dedicated CI/CD pipeline automation server — Chef/Puppet/Ansible are configuration-management tools, a related but different job.

q: A systems administrator requires that all files that are created by the user named web have read-only permissions by the owner. Which of the following commands will satisfy this requirement?
explanation: Adding umask 377 to the user's .bashrc makes every new file automatically read-only for the owner and nothing for others going forward. chown changes ownership not permissions, a one-time chmod only fixes existing files, and the setfacl syntax shown isn't valid.

optExpl.A:
chown changes ownership — it doesn't set default permissions for files the user will create in the future.

Flag breakdown:
  chown web:web → Change owner AND group to 'web' (ownership, not permissions)
optExpl.B:
chmod -R 400 makes existing files read-only right now — it doesn't affect permissions of files created in the future.

Flag breakdown:
  chmod -R 400 → Recursively set all existing files to 400 (r--------)
  (Future files created by the user still get default permissions based on umask)
optExpl.C:
Sets the default creation permissions so every new file is automatically read-only for owner, nothing for others.

Flag breakdown:
  echo 'umask 377' >> ~/.bashrc → Append to user's bash startup file
  umask      → User file creation MASK — subtracted from default permissions
  377        → Mask: 666 (default file permissions) - 377 = 400 (r--------)
    3        → Remove group write+execute
    7        → Remove ALL other permissions (rwx)
    7        → Remove ALL other-other permissions
  Result: new files get permissions 400 (read-only for owner)
  ~/.bashrc  → Runs on every new interactive bash shell — makes umask persistent
optExpl.D:
The setfacl syntax shown is not valid — setfacl requires -m and proper ACL format.

Flag breakdown:
  setfacl read /home/web → Invalid: setfacl syntax is: setfacl -m u:user:permissions path
  (ACL = Access Control List — a more granular permission system beyond owner/group/other)

examTip: umask sets the *default* permission mask applied to every newly created file automatically — the right tool when the requirement is about all *future* files, not a one-time chmod on files that already exist.

q: A systems administrator is tasked with preventing logins from accounts other than root, while the file /etc/ nologin exists. Which of the following PAM modules will accomplish this task?
explanation: pam_nologin.so checks for /etc/nologin and blocks all logins except root when it exists — exactly matching the requirement. pam_login, pam_access, and pam_logindef aren't the PAM module responsible for the /etc/nologin behavior.

optExpl.A: pam_login.so is not a real PAM module name.
optExpl.B: pam_access.so controls access based on user, host, or terminal rules — not /etc/nologin checking.
optExpl.C: pam_logindef.so is not a real PAM module name.
optExpl.D: pam_nologin.so checks for the existence of /etc/nologin and, if present, denies login to all users except root — exactly the described behavior.

examTip: pam_nologin.so is the PAM module that checks for /etc/nologin and blocks all non-root logins while that file exists — purpose-built for exactly this maintenance-mode scenario.

q: A systems administrator has been tasked with disabling the nginx service from the environment to prevent it from being automatically and manually started. Which of the following commands will accomplish this task?
explanation: systemctl mask nginx links the unit to /dev/null, preventing it from being started by any means. disable only stops auto-start (manual start still works), and stop just halts it temporarily.

optExpl.A:
'systemctl cancel' is not a valid systemctl subcommand.

Flag breakdown:
  systemctl  → systemd control tool
  cancel     → Not a real subcommand (try: systemctl --help)
optExpl.B:
systemctl disable prevents auto-start at boot — but the service can STILL be started manually with systemctl start.

Flag breakdown:
  systemctl disable → Removes symlink from target.wants/ (no auto-start at boot)
  (Service remains startable manually — doesn't fully block it)
optExpl.C:
Links the unit file to /dev/null, making it impossible to start by ANY means — manual or automatic.

Flag breakdown:
  systemctl  → systemd control tool
  mask nginx → Create a symlink: /etc/systemd/system/nginx.service → /dev/null
    /dev/null → The null device — discards all data written to it
    Effect: systemd reads the unit as empty — cannot start it by any means
  (Reverse with: systemctl unmask nginx)
  (Stronger than 'disable' — even 'systemctl start nginx' will fail with 'masked')
optExpl.D:
systemctl stop halts the service right now — it can be started again manually or at next boot.

Flag breakdown:
  systemctl stop → Send SIGTERM to service, wait for shutdown
  (Temporary — service restarts at next boot if enabled, or manually with 'start')

examTip: systemctl mask makes a service impossible to start either automatically or manually (it symlinks the unit to /dev/null) — stronger than disable, which only prevents automatic/boot-time starts but still allows a manual start.

q: A Linux administrator is troubleshooting an issue in which an application service failed to start on a Linux server. The administrator runs a few commands and gets the following outputs: Based on the above outputs, which of the following is the MOST likely action the administrator should take to resolve this issue?

options.A: Enable the logsearch.service and restart the service.
options.B: Increase the TimeoutStartUSec configuration for the logsearch.sevice.
options.C: Update the OnCalendar configuration to schedule the start of the logsearch.service.
options.D: Update the KillSignal configuration for the logsearch.service to use TERM.

explanation: TimeoutStartUSec gives a slow-starting service more time to finish initializing before systemd marks it failed. Enabling the unit, adjusting a timer schedule, or changing the kill signal don't address a startup-timeout failure.

optExpl.A: Enabling the service doesn't fix a service that fails because it takes too long to start — enable controls auto-start, not startup timeouts.
optExpl.B: Increasing TimeoutStartUSec gives the service more time to complete initialization before systemd marks it as failed — directly addressing a slow-starting service.
optExpl.C: OnCalendar is a timer unit directive for scheduling — not a configuration for a service's startup behavior.
optExpl.D: KillSignal changes what signal is sent to stop the service — it doesn't affect the startup timeout.

examTip: A service repeatedly failing with a timeout during startup often just needs more time — raise TimeoutStartUSec in the unit file rather than changing scheduling, kill signals, or enablement, none of which address a slow-starting process being killed too early.

q: A Linux administrator has installed a web server, a database server, and a web application on a server. The web application should be active in order to render the web pages. After the administrator restarts the server, the website displays the following message in the browser: Error establishing a database connection. The Linux administrator reviews the following relevant output from the systemd init files: The administrator needs to ensure that the database is available before the web application is started. Which of the following should the administrator add to the HTTP server .service file to accomplish this task?
explanation: Adding Requires=mariadb.service to the web app's unit file creates a hard dependency ensuring systemd starts (and considers healthy) the database before starting the web application. TRIGGERS/ONFAILURE/WANTEDBY don't enforce a strict start-before dependency the way Requires= does.

optExpl.A: TRIGGERS is not a standard systemd unit file directive.
optExpl.B: OnFailure= specifies units to activate when this unit fails — not to require another service to start first.
optExpl.C: WantedBy= is used in the [Install] section to specify which target to link this unit into — not to require another service.
optExpl.D: Requires=mariadb.service in the [Unit] section creates a hard dependency: systemd will start (and require the success of) mariadb.service before starting the web app.

examTip: systemd's Requires= creates a hard dependency — the unit won't start (and stops if the dependency fails) until the required service is up, which is exactly "ensure the database is available before the web app starts." Wants= is only a soft/best-effort hint, not a real prerequisite.

q: Several users reported that they were unable to write data to the /oracle1 directory. The following output has been provided: Which of the following commands should the administrator use to diagnose the issue?
explanation: df -i reports inode usage — if all inodes are consumed even with disk space free, new files can't be created. fdisk/lsblk report partition layout, and du reports how much space existing files use.

optExpl.A:
Reports inode usage — if all inodes are consumed, new files cannot be created even if disk space remains.

Flag breakdown:
  df         → Disk Free — show filesystem space and inode usage
  -i         → Inodes — show inode counts instead of block counts
  /oracle1   → Show inode stats for this specific filesystem/path
  (Inode = Index Node: filesystem metadata entry for each file — each file needs one)
  (If Iuse% = 100%: no more files can be created regardless of free disk space)
  (Compare with df -h /oracle1 to see if disk space is also a factor)
optExpl.B:
fdisk -l shows partition table information — not why writes are failing.

Flag breakdown:
  fdisk -l   → List partition table (size, type, start/end sectors)
optExpl.C:
lsblk shows block device information and relationships — not inode or disk space usage.

Flag breakdown:
  lsblk      → List Block devices (shows disk/partition relationships)
optExpl.D:
du shows disk space USED by existing files — it doesn't reveal inode exhaustion.

Flag breakdown:
  du -sh     → Disk Usage: -s=summary total, -h=human-readable size
  (Shows space used, not whether inode table is full)

examTip: "No space left" errors with plenty of visible disk capacity free are often an inode exhaustion problem, not a block/byte-space problem — df -i checks inode usage specifically, separate from the default df (which reports block/byte usage).

q: After installing some RPM packages, a systems administrator discovers the last package that was installed was not needed. Which of the following commands can be used to remove the package?
explanation: dnf remove packagename is the correct command on RPM-based systems to uninstall a package. apt/apt-get are for Debian-based systems and won't work here, and rpm -i installs rather than removes.

optExpl.A:
Correct uninstall command for RPM (RPM Package Manager)-based Linux systems.

Flag breakdown:
  dnf        → Dandified YUM — package manager for RHEL, CentOS, Fedora
  remove     → Uninstall the package and optionally clean up orphaned deps
  packagename → Name of the package to remove
  (RPM-based distros: RHEL, CentOS, Fedora, AlmaLinux, Rocky Linux)
optExpl.B:
apt-get is for Debian/Ubuntu (DEB-based) systems — it won't work on an RPM-based system.

Flag breakdown:
  apt-get    → Advanced Package Tool — for Debian/Ubuntu (deb-based) systems
  remove     → Uninstall package
optExpl.C:
rpm -i INSTALLS a package — it's the opposite of removal.

Flag breakdown:
  rpm -i     → Install a package from an .rpm file
  (rpm -e packagename → Remove/Erase with the bare rpm command)
optExpl.D:
apt remove is also for Debian/Ubuntu (DEB-based) systems — wrong package manager for this RPM-based environment.

Flag breakdown:
  apt remove → Debian/Ubuntu uninstall command (different package format than RPM)

examTip: Match the package manager to the distro family: dnf/yum for RPM-based systems, apt/apt-get for Debian-based — using rpm -i to install (not remove) or the wrong family's tool won't accomplish an RPM removal.

q: A systems administrator is checking the system logs. The administrator wants to look at the last 20 lines of a log. Which of the following will execute the command?
explanation: tail -n 20 shows the last 20 lines. -v, -c, and -l aren't valid tail flags for line count (-c is byte count).

optExpl.A:
-v is a verbose flag that prints the filename when processing multiple files — not a line count.

Flag breakdown:
  tail -v    → Verbose: print header with filename (useful when tailing multiple files)
optExpl.B:
Shows the last 20 lines of the file.

Flag breakdown:
  tail       → Show end of file
  -n 20      → Number of lines: show last 20 lines
  (Default without -n: shows last 10 lines)
  (tail -n +20 → Show from line 20 to end — different meaning with + prefix)
  (Related: head -n 20 shows first 20 lines)
optExpl.C:
-c 20 shows the last 20 BYTES (characters) — not 20 lines.

Flag breakdown:
  tail -c 20 → Show last 20 Characters/bytes (not lines)
optExpl.D:
-l is not a valid tail flag.

Flag breakdown:
  tail -l    → Not a recognized option for tail

examTip: tail -n <N> prints just the last N lines of a file — the flag to reach for whenever a question specifies an exact line count.

q: An administrator is trying to diagnose a performance issue and is reviewing the following output: System Properties: CPU: 4 vCPU - Memory: 40GB - Disk maximum IOPS: 690 - Disk maximum throughput: 44Mbps | 44000Kbps Based on the above output, which of the following BEST describes the root cause?

options.A: The system has reached its maximum IOPS, causing the system to be slow.
options.B: The system has reached its maximum permitted throughput, therefore iowait is increasing.
options.C: The system is mostly idle, therefore the iowait is high.
options.D: The system has a partitioned disk, which causes the IOPS to be doubled.

explanation: The system has hit its maximum disk throughput ceiling (44Mbps), so I/O requests queue and iowait rises even though IOPS hasn't maxed out — a throughput cap, not an IOPS cap, is the bottleneck based on the numbers. Other options misread which metric is actually maxed.

optExpl.A: If IOPS were maxed out, the IOPS counter would be at its ceiling — the output shows throughput (MB/s) maxed while IOPS still has headroom.
optExpl.B: When disk throughput (MB/s) hits its maximum (44Mbps), I/O requests queue up and iowait rises — the IOPS figure can still appear low while the pipe is saturated.
optExpl.C: An idle system would show low iowait, not high — high iowait means the CPU is waiting for I/O, indicating the system is busy, not idle.
optExpl.D: Partitioning doesn't double IOPS — it distributes workload but doesn't multiply the underlying disk's performance.

examTip: iowait rising while a workload sits at (or near) a cloud disk's documented max throughput/IOPS ceiling means the storage tier itself is the bottleneck — not CPU, not an idle system, and not partitioning.

q: A systems administrator wants to test the route between IP address 10.0.2.15 and IP address 192.168.1.40. Which of the following commands will accomplish this task?
explanation: ip route get traces and reports the specific route the kernel would use between two addresses. The route command syntax in other options is either invalid or doesn't perform this specific from/to lookup.

optExpl.A:
'route -e get to X from Y' is not valid legacy route command syntax.

Flag breakdown:
  route      → Legacy routing command (replaced by ip route in modern Linux)
  -e         → Extended format for route output
optExpl.B:
Traces and shows the exact routing path the kernel would use for a specific source→destination pair.

Flag breakdown:
  ip         → iproute2 network management suite
  route      → Manage routing table
  get        → Show route the kernel would use for a specific destination
  192.168.1.40 → Destination IP address to look up
  from 10.0.2.15 → Source IP to use for the lookup
  (Output shows: next-hop, interface, source address, metric)
  (Useful for debugging: 'why does traffic from X to Y take route Z?')
optExpl.C:
'ip route 192.169.1.40 to 10.0.2.15' has the argument order reversed and uses 'to' incorrectly.

Flag breakdown:
  ip route [action] [destination] → Correct syntax
  192.169.1.40 to 10.0.2.15 → Reversed: destination and source are swapped
optExpl.D:
'route -n X from Y' is not valid route command syntax for this type of lookup.

Flag breakdown:
  route -n   → Show routing table numerically (no DNS resolution)
  (route -n doesn't support from/to source-based lookups)

examTip: ip route get <dest> from <source> asks the kernel's routing table which path it would actually use between two specific addresses — the direct way to "test the route" without sending real traffic.

q: A Linux administrator was tasked with deleting all files and directories with names that are contained in the toDelete.txt file. Which of the following commands will accomplish this task?
explanation: cat toDelete.txt | xargs rm -rf reads each filename from the file and passes them to rm -rf. The other options combine flags or feed cat incorrectly and aren't valid for processing a name list from a file.

optExpl.A:
'xargs -f cat toDelete.txt -rm' is invalid syntax — xargs doesn't use -f and -rm is not a valid flag combination.

Flag breakdown:
  xargs      → Execute a command with arguments from STDIN
  -f         → Not a valid xargs option
optExpl.B:
'rm -d -r -f toDelete.txt' tries to delete the LITERAL FILE named 'toDelete.txt' — not the files listed inside it.

Flag breakdown:
  rm -d -r -f toDelete.txt → Deletes the 'toDelete.txt' file itself
  (To delete files listed INSIDE the file, you need to read its contents with cat | xargs)
optExpl.C:
Pipes the filename list to rm, but rm doesn't read filenames from STDIN — it only accepts filenames as command-line arguments.

Flag breakdown:
  cat toDelete.txt → Outputs list of filenames
  | rm -frd  → rm ignores STDIN (doesn't read filenames from pipe)
  -frd       → Also not standard rm flags (-f=force, -r=recursive, -d=remove empty dirs)
optExpl.D:
Reads each filename from the list file and passes them as command-line arguments to rm.

Flag breakdown:
  cat toDelete.txt → Read contents of the file (list of filenames, one per line)
  |          → Pipe to next command
  xargs      → Build and execute command lines from STDIN input
  rm         → Remove command to run
  -r         → Recursive (delete directories and their contents)
  -f         → Force (no confirmation prompts, don't error on missing files)
  (xargs takes each line from STDIN and passes it as an argument to rm)

examTip: cat <file> | xargs rm -rf feeds each line of a text file as an argument to rm, deleting everything listed — the standard pattern for turning a list-of-names file into a bulk delete.

q: A Linux administrator is troubleshooting the root cause of a high CPU load and average. Which of the following commands will permanently resolve the issue?
chapter: Module 8: Managing the Linux Kernel and Devices
explanation: Killing the runaway process (kill -9) is the only option that actually stops a CPU-monopolizing process. renice only deprioritizes it without stopping it, pstree just visualizes process relationships, and iostat reports I/O statistics rather than addressing CPU load.

optExpl.A:
renice -n -20 gives the highest possible scheduling priority — this makes the process run FASTER, worsening the CPU saturation.

Flag breakdown:
  renice     → Re-NICE — change scheduling priority of running process
  -n -20     → Nice value -20 = HIGHEST priority (range: -20 highest to +19 lowest)
  6295       → Target PID (Process ID)
  (Opposite of what's needed — you'd want renice -n +19 to lower priority, not kill)
optExpl.B:
pstree -p 6295 displays the process tree for that PID — it's a diagnostic tool, not a termination command.

Flag breakdown:
  pstree     → Process TREE — show processes in parent/child hierarchy
  -p         → Show PIDs alongside process names
optExpl.C:
iostat -cy reports disk I/O statistics — completely unrelated to resolving CPU overload from a specific process.

Flag breakdown:
  iostat     → I/O Statistics — disk and CPU utilization reporting
  -c         → CPU statistics
  -y         → Omit first (since-boot) report
  1 5        → Sample every 1 second, 5 times
optExpl.D:
Forcibly terminates the process — the only option here that actually stops the CPU-consuming runaway.

Flag breakdown:
  kill       → Send a signal to a process
  -9         → Signal 9 = SIGKILL (Forced Kill — cannot be caught, blocked, or ignored)
  6295       → Target PID (Process ID)
  (SIGKILL vs SIGTERM:
   kill -15 (SIGTERM) → Polite request to terminate — process can clean up or ignore it
   kill -9  (SIGKILL) → Forced immediate termination — kernel kills it directly)

examTip: kill -9 sends an unblockable, unignorable termination signal that immediately ends a runaway process — renice only lowers its priority (doesn't stop it), and pstree/iostat are just diagnostic, not corrective.

q: A Linux administrator wants to set the SUID of a file named dev_team.text with 744 access rights. Which of the following commands will achieve this goal?
explanation: export ENABLE_AUTH=1 makes the variable available to subsequently executed commands. Plain assignment keeps it shell-local, and let is for arithmetic.

optExpl.A:
Sets the SUID bit using standard numeric notation.

Flag breakdown:
  chmod      → CHange MODe (file permissions)
  4744       → Four-digit octal permission:
    4        → SUID (Set User ID) bit — leading digit
    7        → Owner: rwx (read+write+execute = 4+2+1)
    4        → Group: r-- (read only)
    4        → Others: r-- (read only)
  SUID effect: when executed, the file runs as its OWNER (not the person running it)
  (Verify with: ls -l dev_team.txt — you'll see 's' in owner execute: -rwsr--r--)
optExpl.B:
chmod doesn't have a --setuid flag — SUID is set numerically (leading 4) or symbolically (u+s).

Flag breakdown:
  chmod 744  → Permissions without SUID (no leading 4)
  --setuid   → Not a valid chmod option
  (Correct: chmod 4744 or chmod u+s dev_team.txt)
optExpl.C:
-c makes chmod verbose about changes — it doesn't set SUID. 744 without the leading 4 doesn't include the SUID bit.

Flag breakdown:
  chmod -c   → Report only when a change is made (verbose flag)
  744        → rwxr--r-- (no SUID — missing the leading 4)
optExpl.D:
chmod doesn't have a --suid flag, and -v just makes chmod verbose about changes made.

Flag breakdown:
  chmod -v   → Verbose — output for every file processed
  4744       → Would be correct numerically...
  --suid     → But this flag doesn't exist and would cause an error

examTip: chmod's numeric mode encodes special bits as a leading digit: 4 = SUID, 2 = SGID, 1 = sticky — so SUID + rwxr--r-- (744) is written as 4744, prefixed onto the normal three-digit permission set.

q: Users report that they are unable to reach the company website https://www.comptia.org. A systems administrator confirms the issue: `curl https://www.comptia.org` returns "curl: (7) Failed to connect to www.comptia.org port 443: No route to host". On the web server, `firewall-cmd --list-all` shows the active zone's services as "cockpit dhcpv6-client http ssh" (no https), and `ip route` shows a correct default route via eth0. Which of the following is causing the issue?

options.A: The web server's interface has no link.
options.B: The default route on the web server is incorrect.
options.C: HTTPS traffic is not allowed through the web server firewall.
options.D: User IP addresses are rejected by the firewall.

explanation: firewall-cmd --list-all shows the active zone permits http and ssh but not https, so the host firewall is dropping port 443/tcp before it ever reaches the web server process -- matching curl's "No route to host" (firewalld's reject behavior). Fix: `firewall-cmd --add-service=https --permanent && firewall-cmd --reload`.

optExpl.A: eth0 shows an active default route (`default via ... dev eth0`) in the ip route output, so the interface has link and is configured -- this isn't a down-interface problem.
optExpl.B: The routing table already has a correct default route. A bad default route would break most outbound traffic, not selectively block just HTTPS.
optExpl.C: The firewalld zone's service list is "cockpit dhcpv6-client http ssh" -- https is missing, so port 443/tcp is blocked at the host firewall. Adding the https service (or opening 443/tcp directly) resolves it.
optExpl.D: The zone's rich rules only reject SSH traffic from specific source IPs -- they don't touch HTTPS, and nothing here points to the affected users being on that list.

examTip: When a service is unreachable but routing and the interface both check out, check the host firewall's service/port list (`firewall-cmd --list-all`) before assuming a network-layer problem -- a missing service entry is a common, easy-to-miss cause.

q: A systems administrator needs to integrate a new storage array into the company's existing storage pool and wants to confirm the operating system detects the new array. Which of the following commands should the administrator use?
explanation: lsscsi lists SCSI-layer devices (which includes most enterprise storage arrays), making it the direct way to confirm the OS sees a newly attached array.

optExpl.A: lsscsi lists recognized SCSI devices and their device nodes -- the tool built specifically for verifying storage-array detection at the SCSI layer.
optExpl.B: lsusb only enumerates USB devices, not SCSI/SATA/SAS storage arrays.
optExpl.C: lsipc reports on inter-process communication facilities (shared memory, semaphores) -- unrelated to hardware detection.
optExpl.D: lshw shows broad hardware details and could include storage, but lsscsi is the purpose-built, more direct tool for this specific check.

examTip: lsscsi is the go-to command whenever a question is specifically about confirming a storage array/SCSI device was detected -- lshw is the generic "show me everything" fallback, not the first choice.

q: Users report that they cannot access some files located in the /opt/finapp directory after a power outage caused an unexpected server restart. The administrator finds /opt/finapp is an XFS filesystem, and /var/log/messages shows "XFS (opt_finapp): Corruption detected in inode 3645, extent tree." Which of the following commands should the administrator run in an attempt to fix the filesystem?
explanation: XFS has its own dedicated repair tool -- xfs_repair -- and does not use fsck; fsck.ext4 only works on ext-family filesystems, and the corruption message explicitly names XFS.

optExpl.A: fdisk edits partition tables, not filesystem structures -- it can't repair corruption inside an already-created filesystem.
optExpl.B: xfs_repair is XFS's dedicated consistency-check-and-repair tool, built specifically for the "corruption detected in inode/extent tree" scenario described here.
optExpl.C: This mixes lvcreate (which makes a brand-new logical volume, destroying data) with an ext4 tool -- neither belongs in an XFS repair, and running it would make things worse.
optExpl.D: fsck.ext4 only understands ext2/3/4 filesystems; running it against an XFS filesystem does nothing useful.

examTip: Match the repair tool to the filesystem type: XFS uses xfs_repair, ext2/3/4 uses fsck.ext4/e2fsck -- mixing them up is a common distractor.

q: An administrator logs in to a Linux server and notices the clock is 37 minutes fast. Which of the following commands will fix the issue?
explanation: ntpdate performs an immediate, one-shot time correction against an NTP server -- the direct fix for a clock that's already drifted noticeably out of sync.

optExpl.A: hwclock reads/sets the hardware (RTC) clock directly, but doesn't sync against a time server to correct drift.
optExpl.B: ntpdate immediately queries an NTP server and steps the system clock to match -- the quickest way to correct a clock that's already 37 minutes off.
optExpl.C: timedatectl manages systemd's time settings (timezone, NTP on/off) but doesn't itself force an immediate one-shot correction the way ntpdate does.
optExpl.D: ntpd -q performs a one-time sync-and-exit similar to ntpdate, but ntpdate is the more direct, purpose-built command for this exact scenario.

examTip: For a clock that's already drifted out of sync, reach for a one-shot correction tool (ntpdate/ntpd -q) -- timedatectl and hwclock manage settings and hardware time, not an active resync.

q: A Linux administrator is working with a CPU-intensive program called data-analysis1 and needs to prevent it from monopolizing CPU resources when it's launched. Which of the following commands accomplishes this?
chapter: Module 8: Managing the Linux Kernel and Devices
explanation: nice <command> launches a program with a lower (less favorable) default scheduling priority, exactly what's needed to keep a CPU-heavy program from crowding out everything else.

optExpl.A: --nice isn't a flag the program itself understands -- nice has to be the command that launches the program, not an argument passed to the program.
optExpl.B: nice data-analysis1 starts the program with a raised (less favorable) niceness value by default, reducing its scheduling priority relative to other processes.
optExpl.C: nice -15 actually *increases* priority (negative-style adjustment via -N syntax needs care; -15 here is ambiguous/incorrect usage) and isn't the safe default way to de-prioritize a new process.
optExpl.D: Launching in the background with & and then running nice afterward as a separate, unrelated command doesn't apply niceness to data-analysis1 at all.

examTip: nice <command> (no dash, plain launch) applies a sane, safer default de-prioritization; renice is the tool for adjusting a process that's already running.

q: A systems administrator engineer wants to configure a Linux server's time zone to America/Chicago. Which of the following commands should the engineer use?
explanation: timedatectl set-timezone <zone> is systemd's standard command for changing a system's configured time zone.

optExpl.A: date only displays/sets the current date and time -- it has no timezone-configuration subcommand.
optExpl.B: set-timezone isn't a standalone command on its own; timezone changes go through timedatectl.
optExpl.C: "time date set" isn't a real command sequence on Linux.
optExpl.D: timedatectl set-timezone America/Chicago is the correct, standard systemd command for changing the configured time zone.

examTip: timedatectl is the modern systemd tool for anything involving date, time, timezone, and NTP sync state -- memorize it as your first guess for time-configuration questions.

q: A Linux administrator is updating the file that contains the addresses of the software and update repositories on an Ubuntu system. Which of the following files should the administrator edit?
explanation: /etc/apt/sources.list is Debian/Ubuntu's list of package repository sources -- yum.conf and dnf.conf are the RPM-family equivalents, not applicable on Ubuntu.

optExpl.A: /etc/apt/sources.list is exactly where apt-based systems (Debian/Ubuntu) list their repository sources.
optExpl.B: listchanges.conf configures the apt-listchanges notification tool, not repository locations.
optExpl.C: yum.conf is the repository/config file for yum -- a RPM-family (RHEL/CentOS/Fedora) tool, not used on Ubuntu.
optExpl.D: dnf.conf is dnf's config file -- again RPM-family, not Ubuntu's package manager.

examTip: Match the config file family to the distro: apt/sources.list for Debian-based systems, yum.conf/dnf.conf (and /etc/yum.repos.d/) for RPM-based systems -- a fast way to eliminate half the options on any package-manager question.

q: A Linux administrator needs to replace the entire content of the test1.sh file with the content of the test2.sh file. Which of the following commands will achieve this goal?
explanation: A single > redirect overwrites the destination file's existing content; >> would append instead of replace.

optExpl.A: >> appends to the end of test1.sh, keeping its old content alongside the new -- not a full replacement.
optExpl.B: A single > redirects and overwrites test1.sh's content entirely with test2.sh's content, exactly "replace."
optExpl.C: < redirects input *into* the cat command rather than writing output to a file -- it doesn't write to test1.sh at all.
optExpl.D: "?" isn't a valid redirection operator.

examTip: Redirection operators: > overwrites, >> appends -- mixing these up is one of the most common shell scripting exam traps.

q: A Linux administrator attempts to log in to a server over SSH as root and receives the error "Permission denied, please try again." The administrator can log in to the console directly as root and confirms the password is correct. Reviewing the SSH configuration shows PermitRootLogin is set to prohibit-password. Which of the following will most likely allow the administrator to log in over SSH as root?

options.A: Log out other user sessions because only one is allowed at a time.
options.B: Enable PAM and configure the SSH module.
options.C: Modify the SSH port to use 2222.
options.D: Use a key to log in as root over SSH.

explanation: PermitRootLogin prohibit-password (a common hardening default) allows root to log in over SSH only via key-based authentication -- password auth for root is deliberately rejected even though the password itself is correct.

optExpl.A: Concurrent-session limits aren't what prohibit-password controls -- this doesn't address the actual restriction in effect.
optExpl.B: PAM is likely already enabled by default; the SSH daemon's PermitRootLogin setting, not a missing PAM module, is what's blocking password-based root login here.
optExpl.C: Changing the port affects which port sshd listens on, not which authentication methods are accepted for root.
optExpl.D: With PermitRootLogin prohibit-password, root can still log in over SSH -- but only using a key, never a password. Setting up key-based auth resolves it.

examTip: "Permission denied" for root over SSH with a *confirmed-correct* password almost always means PermitRootLogin is set to prohibit-password (or without-password) -- the fix is a key, not a password reset.

q: An organization's business office needs to collaborate on quarterly reports and asks the systems administrator to create a finance group. The administrator creates a directory (currently drwxrwxr-x, group "Business") for this purpose. Which of the following commands will allow all members of the finance group to have group ownership of all files created in the directory, while ensuring members of the business group preserve access? (Select two).
explanation: Changing the directory's group to Finance (chgrp) and setting the setgid bit (chmod g+s) together make every new file created inside automatically group-owned by Finance -- the standard combination for shared-directory group inheritance.

optExpl.A: chgrp Finance Q1/ changes the directory's own group to Finance, the group new files should inherit.
optExpl.B: chmod g+s Q1/ (setgid) makes every new file/subdirectory created inside automatically take on the directory's group -- without this, chgrp alone only affects the directory itself, not future files.
optExpl.C: setuid (u+s) on a directory has no effect on group-ownership inheritance -- it's a different, unrelated bit.
optExpl.D: a+x only affects execute (traverse) permission for everyone; it doesn't touch group ownership or inheritance.
optExpl.E: chown changes the *owner*, not the group -- the requirement here is about group ownership, so chgrp is the correct tool, not chown.
optExpl.F: g+x only affects execute permission for the existing group; it doesn't change which group a new file inherits.

examTip: "New files should automatically belong to the shared group" is the signature phrase for setgid (chmod g+s) on a directory -- almost always paired with chgrp to first set the group you want inherited.
source: VCE dump, answer independently determined (source PDF did not include an extractable answer key for this question).

q: A systems administrator updates a DNS zone file to point www.abc.com to a new IP address, but querying it still returns the old IP mapping. Which of the following should the administrator run on the client to retrieve the updated IP mapping?
explanation: A stale DNS answer after the authoritative record has already changed points to a local resolver cache still holding the old value -- resolvectl flush-caches clears systemd-resolved's cache so the next query re-fetches fresh data.

optExpl.A: "systemd-resolve query" isn't valid syntax for the modern resolvectl-based tool, and querying again would still hit the same stale cache anyway.
optExpl.B: systemd-resolve status reports resolver configuration/state -- it's informational and doesn't clear any cached records.
optExpl.C: nslcd is for LDAP-based name service lookups, unrelated to DNS resolver caching.
optExpl.D: resolvectl flush-caches clears systemd-resolved's local DNS cache, forcing the next lookup to fetch the current (updated) record instead of a stale cached one.

examTip: When an authoritative DNS record was already changed but clients still see the old value, suspect a local resolver *cache*, not the zone file -- flushing the cache (resolvectl flush-caches) is the fix, not editing DNS again.

q: A Linux server is not starting up because files in the /boot/ partition are corrupt. After the initial GRUB screen, the message "Uncompression error -- System halted" is displayed. Which of the following steps should the administrator take to recover the system without destroying the existing installation? (Select two).

options.B: Increase the amount of swap memory.
options.D: Start up the system using rescue boot media.

explanation: With /boot itself corrupt, the system can't reach any normal boot target (including single-user mode) -- recovery means booting external rescue media first, then reinstalling/regenerating the kernel files that live in /boot.

optExpl.A: The hard drive isn't reported as failed, just the boot files -- replacing hardware is a drastic, unnecessary step.
optExpl.B: Swap size has nothing to do with a GRUB-stage uncompression error reading corrupted /boot files.
optExpl.C: Single-user mode is still a normal boot target reached *after* the kernel/initrd load successfully -- if /boot itself is corrupt, the system can't get that far.
optExpl.D: Booting from rescue media gives you a working environment to mount the broken system's filesystems and repair /boot without needing the (currently unbootable) installed OS.
optExpl.E: From the rescue environment, reinstalling the kernel package regenerates the corrupted vmlinuz/initrd files in /boot, restoring a bootable state.
optExpl.F: A full OS reinstall would work but destroys the existing installation and all its configuration/data -- the question specifically asks to avoid that.

examTip: "Recover without destroying the existing installation" is the tell to reach for rescue/live boot media plus a targeted repair (like reinstalling just the kernel package) -- not a full reinstall, and not a boot mode that itself depends on the broken files.
source: VCE dump, answer independently determined (source PDF did not include an extractable answer key for this question).

q: An administrator has generated an RSA SSH key pair to log in to a remote server. After copying the public key and attempting to log in, the administrator sees "Permission denied (publickey,password)" and debug output showing "send_pubkey_test: no mutual signature algorithm." Which of the following actions should the administrator take first to remediate this issue?

options.A: Issue systemctl restart sshd on the local server.
options.B: Create a new key pair by running ssh-keygen -t ecdsa.
options.C: Set PermitRootLogin yes in the /etc/ssh/sshd_config file.
options.D: Update permissions on the /home/admin/.ssh directory to 700 on the remote server.

explanation: "No mutual signature algorithm" means the client and server don't share a compatible key-signing algorithm -- modern OpenSSH versions disable the older ssh-rsa signature scheme by default, so switching to a modern key type (ecdsa/ed25519) resolves the mismatch.

optExpl.A: Restarting sshd on the local machine doesn't change which signature algorithms either side is willing to negotiate.
optExpl.B: Generating a key with a currently-accepted signature algorithm (ecdsa) sidesteps the deprecated-ssh-rsa mismatch causing the negotiation failure.
optExpl.C: PermitRootLogin controls whether root specifically can log in -- it's unrelated to a signature-algorithm negotiation failure, and this scenario doesn't even mention the root account.
optExpl.D: Loose .ssh directory permissions cause SSH to silently ignore authorized_keys, not this specific "no mutual signature algorithm" negotiation error.

examTip: "No mutual signature algorithm" is a specific, recognizable phrase pointing at an incompatible/deprecated key type (classic ssh-rsa) -- not a permissions or config problem; regenerating with a modern algorithm (ecdsa/ed25519) is the fix.

q: A systems administrator is compressing old log files to save as much disk space as possible, and compression time is not a concern. Which of the following commands will achieve the best compression ratio?
explanation: Of the common Linux compressors, xz (LZMA2-based) typically achieves the best compression ratio at the cost of being the slowest -- the right tradeoff when space matters more than speed.

optExpl.A: bzip2 generally compresses better than gzip but not as well as xz.
optExpl.B: xz achieves the highest compression ratio of these options, trading extra CPU time/speed for smaller output -- ideal when "time is not a concern."
optExpl.C: tar only bundles files together (archiving); it doesn't compress on its own without a compression flag/pipe.
optExpl.D: gzip is fast but has the weakest compression ratio of the three actual compressors listed here.

examTip: Rank of compression ratio (best to fastest) among gzip/bzip2/xz: xz compresses smallest but slowest, gzip is fastest but compresses least -- pick based on which the question says matters more, space or time.

q: An application requires a configuration file to be placed in each user's home directory automatically whenever a new account is created. In which of the following locations should the administrator place this file?
explanation: Anything placed in /etc/skel is automatically copied into a new user's home directory when useradd -m creates it -- the standard mechanism for seeding default per-user files.

optExpl.A: /etc/skel is the "skeleton" directory whose contents are copied into every newly created user's home directory -- exactly the mechanism this scenario needs.
optExpl.B: /etc/sysconfig holds system-wide service/network configuration, not per-user home directory templates.
optExpl.C: /etc/ssh holds SSH daemon/client configuration, unrelated to new-user home directory content.
optExpl.D: /etc/rc.local (where still used) runs commands at boot -- it's not a per-user file template location.

examTip: /etc/skel is the exam's standard answer whenever a question is about files that should automatically appear in every new user's home directory.

q: An administrator thinks the user Joe may be running an unauthorized process on a Linux server. Which of the following commands should the administrator use to view Joe's running processes and their live resource usage?
chapter: Module 8: Managing the Linux Kernel and Devices
explanation: top -u <user> filters the live, continuously-updating process view down to just that user's processes -- the right tool for actively watching what a specific user is running.

optExpl.A: lsof -p expects a PID, not a username, and lists open files rather than giving a live resource-usage view.
optExpl.B: top -u 'Joe' filters top's live, auto-refreshing display to only Joe's processes -- exactly what's needed to watch what a specific user is currently running.
optExpl.C: jobs lists background jobs of the *current shell session*, not another user's processes system-wide, and doesn't take a username filter this way.
optExpl.D: ps -ax lists all processes system-wide but doesn't filter by username with that syntax, and it's a static snapshot rather than a live view.

examTip: top -u <user> is the quick way to watch one user's processes live; ps -u <user> would give a similar filtered *snapshot* instead of a continuously refreshing view -- know the distinction between live monitoring and a one-time listing.

q: A systems administrator is writing a script to report the number of files in a given directory. Which of the following commands, piped from an `ls` listing, will produce a simple count?
explanation: wc -l counts lines in its input -- piping a one-file-per-line `ls` listing into wc -l is the standard way to count files in a directory from a script.

optExpl.A: less is a pager for viewing output interactively; it doesn't produce a count.
optExpl.B: tail -f follows a growing file/stream for new lines -- it's for watching live output, not counting existing entries.
optExpl.C: tr translates or deletes characters; it isn't a counting tool on its own.
optExpl.D: wc -l counts the number of lines in its input -- piping ls (one entry per line) into wc -l gives a simple file count.

examTip: wc -l is the standard "count lines/items" tool in a pipeline -- reach for it whenever a script needs to turn a line-per-item listing into a number.

q: A systems administrator is deploying a web server using the following code snippet: `name "Web Server" description "The role contains nodes, which act as a web server"`. Which of the following technologies is the administrator using?
explanation: "Roles" defined with name/description attributes in a Ruby-flavored DSL is Chef's distinctive syntax style -- Ansible uses YAML playbooks, Puppet uses its own declarative manifest language, and Terraform uses HCL.

optExpl.A: Chef defines roles using exactly this kind of Ruby-based DSL block (name/description/run_list) -- the syntax shown is characteristic of a Chef role definition.
optExpl.B: Ansible's playbooks are written in YAML, not this Ruby-style attribute block.
optExpl.C: Puppet manifests use their own declarative resource syntax, visually distinct from this Chef-style role block.
optExpl.D: Terraform uses HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language) for declaring infrastructure resources -- a different syntax entirely.

examTip: Recognize each config-management tool by its file syntax on sight: Ansible = YAML playbooks, Chef = Ruby-based DSL (recipes/roles/cookbooks), Puppet = its own declarative manifest language, Terraform = HCL.

q: Which of the following RAID levels represents disk mirroring?
explanation: RAID 1 writes an identical copy of all data to two (or more) disks -- the definition of mirroring.

optExpl.A: RAID 0 is striping for performance, with no redundancy at all -- the opposite of mirroring.
optExpl.B: RAID 1 duplicates all data across two or more drives in real time -- exactly what "mirroring" means.
optExpl.C: RAID 5 uses striping with distributed parity, not a full duplicate copy.
optExpl.D: RAID 6 is like RAID 5 with an extra parity block for additional fault tolerance, still parity-based rather than a mirror.

examTip: Memorize the core RAID identities: 0 = striping (speed, no redundancy), 1 = mirroring (full duplicate), 5/6 = striping with (single/double) parity.

q: A Linux systems administrator wants to validate the network interface configuration and status for the interface eth3 on a server. Which of the following commands should the administrator use?
explanation: ip addr show dev <iface> is the correct modern-iproute2 syntax for displaying one interface's address/status details.

optExpl.A: "ip list interface" isn't valid ip command syntax.
optExpl.B: ip addr show dev eth3 is the correct syntax to display address and status information for a specific interface.
optExpl.C: "ip show" without the addr/link object keyword isn't valid syntax.
optExpl.D: "ip config" isn't a real ip subcommand (that's the older, separate ifconfig tool's naming, not ip's).

examTip: The ip command's syntax pattern is `ip <object> <command> [dev <interface>]` -- e.g. ip addr show dev eth3, ip link show dev eth3 -- memorizing that object-first structure rules out most made-up-looking distractor syntax.

q: A systems administrator needs to check the size of the filesystem on the current application servers, including how much space is used and available on each mounted filesystem. Which of the following commands should the administrator use?
explanation: df reports space usage and availability per mounted filesystem -- du instead reports space used by specific files/directories, a different (and commonly confused) tool.

optExpl.A: fdisk manages partition tables; it doesn't report filesystem space usage.
optExpl.B: df reports total/used/available space for each mounted filesystem -- exactly what's asked for here.
optExpl.C: du reports disk usage of files and directories (a bottom-up sum), not overall filesystem-level free space -- a frequently confused pair with df.
optExpl.D: lsblk lists block devices and their mount points/sizes, but not live used/available space the way df does.

examTip: df = filesystem-level free/used space (top-down); du = space consumed by specific files/directories (bottom-up) -- confusing the two is one of the most common exam traps.
